articles.title: NEWS: Findel Becomes Largest UK Educational Resources Supplier To Be Certified As A Carbon Neutral Business | Dealer Support
articles.author: Dealer Support
articles.content:
Educational resources supplier Findel has officially been certified as a Carbon Neutral Business by Carbon Neutral Britain
The certification confirms Findel has measured its emissions, reduced them in real terms and only offset the remainder through independently verified carbon reduction projects.
Findel’s carbon neutral status covers all operations under Findel Education, including its Nottingham distribution centre, offices and distribution activity.
It also means Findel is the UK’s largest educational resources supplier to be certified as a Carbon Neutral Business.
The certification is valid for 12 months from the date of issue and, after this, Findel will re-measure, reduce and recertify annually.
Findel measured total organisational emissions of 1,095.47 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO2e) across its operations and a defined set of day-to-day business activities categorised under ‘Scopes’.
Scope 1 covers direct emissions from Findel’s own operations, while Scope 2 relates to the electricity it buys to run its sites.
The Scope 3 boundary for the certification includes day-to-day business activity such as staff working from home, waste, business travel, commuting, stays at hotels and events and water usage.
To reduce emissions, Findel rolled out a range of initiatives across its operations. These included the installation of a WirePas-enabled smart building management system at its Nottingham distribution centre, as well as the sourcing of renewable electricity and green gas.
Last year, Findel delivered more than 300,000 parcels using electric-only vehicles, while the introduction of custom-size packaging is reducing carbon by around 46% and material use by around 45 per cent.
The company has also transitioned its truck fleet from LPG to electric and switched diesel to HVO, a renewable diesel alternative, for on-site plant.
Since 2019, Findel has cut its operational energy use by half (49.5 per cent), from 4,600,060 kWh to 2,321,892 kWh in FY25.
Over the same period, Findel cut its market-based operational carbon emissions by 97.7 per cent, from 1,029 tonnes in FY20 to 24 tonnes in FY25.
Findel selected a mix of UK and international carbon reduction projects to balance environmental and social benefits across its customer base.
UK-based projects include native tree planting, hay meadow restoration and seagrass meadow restoration. International projects support renewable energy generation in developing countries.
Commenting on the certification, Findel chief executive, Chris Mahady, said: “Schools, nurseries and trusts are increasingly looking for clear evidence of sustainability progress from their suppliers.
“Our customers can be safe in the knowledge that we are measuring our carbon emissions impact, reducing them in real terms and taking responsibility where we can’t yet eliminate it entirely.
“This certification gives them confidence they are working with a partner that is dedicated to taking those responsibilities seriously.”
The certification comes after Findel was accepted onto The Climate Pledge in 2024, committing to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040.
Chris Leonard, ESG manager at Findel, added: “Our customers can be assured knowing they are working with a supplier that prioritises both people and planet.
“This is an important milestone in our wider ESG pathway, not a one-off certification, and we remain committed to driving our own carbon emissions footprint down as far as possible.
“We especially want to use our experience to support customers as they work towards their own sustainability goals. We will do this through clearer information, more responsible product choices and practical partnerships.”
Findel is part of the Manutan Group and is working closely with Manutan’s CSR team to accelerate progress.
Priorities include supplier engagement to support emissions measurement and science-based targets, improving product environmental transparency, and developing circular economy initiatives such as durable design, reduced packaging and reuse schemes.
Headquartered in Hyde, Greater Manchester, Findel also has a distribution centre and offices in Nottingham and employs around 300 people.
For more information on Findel visit www.findel.co.uk
articles.summary: Educational resources supplier Findel has officially been certified as a Carbon Neutral Business by Carbon Neutral Britain The certification confirms Findel has measured its emissions, reduced them in real terms and only offset the remainder through independently verified carbon reduction projects. Findel’s carbon neutral status covers all operations under Findel Education, including its Nottingham distribution centre, offices and distribution activity.

articles.title: Frontiers | Modeling China carbon-certified garlic supply chain under EU low-carbon policies: evolutionary game insights into investment decisions and consumer preferences
articles.author: Frontiers
articles.content:
Abstract
In the context of stricter EU low-carbon policies and increasing consumer demand for sustainable products, this study investigates the evolutionary dynamics of the carbon-certified agricultural export supply chain between China and the EU. A four-party evolutionary game model is developed to analyze the strategic interactions among Chinese garlic suppliers, Chinese export manufacturers, EU suppliers, and EU consumers. Equilibrium and stability analysis are combined with numerical simulations to examine the dynamic evolution of strategic choices under different parameter settings. The results identify threshold conditions under which the supply chain converges to a full green equilibrium, stabilizes at a partially green state, or remains non-certified. Stronger consumer green preference and tighter trade-policy pressure jointly increase the likelihood of a certified low-carbon equilibrium, whereas high certification costs or weak market signals tend to sustain a high-carbon outcome. The findings further show that small changes around key parameters, such as certification cost, tariff pressure, and preference intensity, can trigger regime shifts in long-run strategies. These results provide actionable insights for policymakers and managers on how to align incentives and market signals to facilitate low-carbon transitions in cross-border agri-food supply chains.
1 Introduction
China and the European Union (EU) maintain a vibrant agricultural trading relationship, exemplified by China's dominance in agricultural exports such as garlic. China is the world's largest garlic producer and exporter, shipping roughly 2 million tons globally in 2022 (World Bank, 2022). The EU relies on imports to meet its garlic demand, about 0.2 million tons annually, with China serving as a key supplier. In 2022, China accounted for approximately 25.5% of the EU's extra-EU imports of the “onions and garlic” category, making it the leading external source (Eurostat, 2023). However, this trade is shaped by long-term measures: the EU imposes a tariff-rate quota capping annual garlic imports from China at around 48,225 tons (United States International Trade Commission, 2023), along with anti-dumping measures. Overall, China's agricultural export portfolio to Europe has grown in value and variety in recent years, but remains concentrated in labor-intensive products where China holds a comparative advantage. However, despite this significance, the EU has long imposed strict trade measures, including a tariff-rate quota and anti-dumping duties, creating a highly competitive yet challenging market environment for Chinese garlic exporters.
The EU has, since 2020, launched an ambitious suite of policies to green its agri-food system and reduce the carbon footprint of products sold in its market, as mapped in Figure 1. A cornerstone is the Farm to Fork Strategy (2020) under the European Green Deal, which aims to make food systems “fair, healthy and environmentally-friendly” and climate-neutral by mid-century (Clean Energy Wire, 2021; European Commission, 2020). Alongside Farm to Fork, the EU is developing supporting regulations, such as a legislative framework for sustainable food systems, and considering requirements for carbon footprint disclosure on food labels. At the border-policy level, the EU has introduced the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), a landmark climate-trade policy adopted in 2023. CBAM introduces a carbon price on carbon-intensive imports by requiring importers to purchase certificates reflecting the CO2 emissions embedded in certain goods (European Commission, 2023). In parallel, the European Commission has spearheaded the Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) method as a standard for measuring product-level environmental impact to quantify a product's environmental footprint in a standardized way (European Commission Joint Research Centre, 2021). These policies mandate stricter carbon footprint disclosures, certification processes, and impose implicit carbon costs, profoundly reshaping the competitiveness and resilience of non-EU agricultural supply chains, all of which raise the bar for agricultural exporters to prove and improve the sustainability of their supply chains.
Figure 1
These EU low-carbon policies reshape cross-border agri-food supply chains by affecting both the supply side and the demand side. Specifically, they alter the incentives and constraints faced by upstream Chinese suppliers and exporters on the supply side, while simultaneously shifting EU consumers' purchase decisions and demand patterns on the demand side. As a result, their effects are expected to ripple through global agri-food trade, with developing-country exporters, such as Chinese garlic exporters, being particularly exposed. The visibility of carbon certifications on food products can influence consumer choice in importing countries. Surveys across multiple EU countries show that many consumers are willing to pay a price premium for foods labeled with a low carbon footprint or climate-friendly farming methods (Feucht and Zander, 2017). Although skepticism about “greenwashing” and label fatigue remains a challenge, the overall direction is clear.
In this study, to analyze these multi-actor strategic adaptations under bounded rationality, we employ evolutionary game theory. The four players in our setting, Chinese suppliers, Chinese exporters, EU suppliers, and EU consumers, are considered boundedly rational and update their strategies over time based on limited information and observed payoffs. Evolutionary game theory (EGT), first introduced by Maynard Smith and Price (1973), provides a framework to study how strategies evolve over repeated interactions and which outcomes become stable equilibria (Maynard Smith and Price, 1973; Xia, 2022). This study, therefore, aims to examine the low-carbon certified garlic export supply chain, which is depicted in Figure 2, identifying the factors that influence each participant's decision-making.
Figure 2
Based on the data on China's garlic exports to the EU and the suite of EU low-carbon policies, and assuming bounded rationality among supply-chain participants, alongside current trends in organic produce, it is reasonable to anticipate that carbon-certified retail agricultural products will soon become mainstream. In particular, this paper examines how consumer's low-carbon preferences interact with upstream supply chain investments in determining the chain's evolution toward a fully certified, low-carbon equilibrium.
By solving and simulating the evolutionary game, we address questions such as:
(1) Will the Chinese supplier and the Chinese Exporter have incentives to undertake the relevant investments under EU policy and consumer preference? And to what extent do consumer preferences and associated psychological expectations influence upstream decisions in the export supply chain?
(2) How can the alignment of incentives and the design of cooperative mechanisms among all parties be better aligned to make a fully carbon-certified, low-carbon export supply chain viable and stable over time?
(3) Based on the equilibrium and sensitivity results, what actionable policy and managerial implications can be drawn to facilitate a transition toward a viable low-carbon, carbon-certified garlic export supply chain?
2 Literature review
This study covers four areas: the low-carbon agricultural supply chain and technological investment; labor-efficiency investment in the low-carbon agricultural supply chain; consumer's low-carbon preferences in the supply chain; and evolutionary game applications in low-carbon agricultural supply chains.
2.1 Technological investment in the low-carbon agricultural supply chain
A low-carbon agricultural supply chain refers to an agricultural supply chain that explicitly incorporates carbon emissions into production, processing, cold-chain operations, and distribution decisions, aiming to reduce emissions while maintaining product quality and freshness. Recent studies have increasingly examined how carbon policies and market mechanisms shape low-carbon decisions in agricultural settings. For instance, under a carbon tax, agricultural supply-chain members' emission-reduction choices and cooperative investment behaviors have been modeled to show how cost-sharing and joint investment can improve both economic and environmental outcomes (Liu et al., 2021). In fresh agricultural products, cap-and-trade regulations have been linked to firms' fresh-keeping and coordination decisions, demonstrating how carbon pricing and contract design jointly affect operational effort and profit allocation (Yang and Yao, 2024). Policy-driven incentives have also been incorporated into agri-food supply-chain games; for example, subsidy schemes can alter the dynamic balance between emission reduction and preservation efforts across tiers (He and Yang, 2023). More recently, Nash-based frameworks have been proposed to implement low-carbon schemes in agricultural supply-chain management through multi-actor interaction and coordinated market structures (Hamidoglu and Weber, 2024). Taken together, recent work suggests that agricultural decarbonization depends critically on investment and coordination decisions across supply-chain tiers.
At the firm level, research has examined how supply chain structure, contracts, and incentives drive low-carbon technological adoption, especially in settings where emission reduction interacts with freshness preservation. Under carbon cap-and-trade and consumers' dual preferences, for example, coordination contracts such as cost-sharing and two-part pricing have been shown to affect suppliers' low-carbon and fresh-keeping efforts as well as channel outcomes in fresh agricultural product supply chains (Yang and Yao, 2023). In agricultural settings with insurance support, independent farmers profitably adopt low-carbon cultivation techniques, while outsourcing models yield higher technology uptake when subsidy rates and service-provider cost advantages are sufficiently large (Shi and Wang, 2023). Under carbon tax regimes, enterprises show a stronger preference for efficient low-carbon technologies, with production and transportation emission-reduction investments offering the greatest cost effectiveness (Huang et al., 2020). Moreover, the diffusion of green agricultural technologies also depends on organizational arrangements and policy instruments: comparing contract farming with cooperatives (Gu et al., 2024).
While these contributions establish a rich foundation for understanding low-carbon technological investment in supply chains, they largely treat investment decisions as static or one-stage optimizations. They do not capture how multiple supply chain actors, suppliers, manufacturers, competitors, and consumers dynamically adjust their strategies under evolving carbon regulations and market signals.
2.2 Labor-efficiency investment in the low-carbon agricultural supply chain
In agricultural systems, labor-efficiency investment refers to the deployment of technologies and practices, such as mechanized harvesting, cold-chain logistics, automated sorting, and workforce training, that enhance productivity, reduce post-harvest losses, and improve product consistency (Mustafa et al., 2024). Accordingly, labor-efficiency investment is targeted to raise effective labor productivity across handling, storage, and distribution, thereby supporting both cost and emissions-efficiency goals (de Castro Moura Duarte et al., 2025).
From a modeling perspective, recent network-based studies have begun to treat labor not only as a background condition but as an explicit constraint in agri-food supply chains. Nagurney's study developed a perishable goods network framework incorporating explicit labor availability constraints across production, transportation, storage, and distribution stages to assess resilience under epidemic-induced disruptions (Nagurney, 2021). Extending this, a multi-period network model embedded investments in worker safety and health, interpreted as labor-productivity enhancements, and employed net-present-value analysis to show that, when end-users respond to improved working conditions, such investments yield mutual gains for firms and workers (Nagurney, 2021). These studies provide a clear methodological basis for modeling labor-efficiency as an investable, dynamic driver of perishable supply-chain performance.
Beyond modeling labor as a constraint, recent low-carbon agri-food and cold-chain studies increasingly recognize that workforce capability and skills are a central bottleneck for sustainability performance, motivating investments in training, standardized operating procedures, and technology-enabled workflows. For example, systematic reviews of perishable food cold-chain logistics identify workforce skill shortages as a recurring challenge, implying that improving labor productivity and execution quality is essential to reduce avoidable losses and resource waste (Zhang and Mohammad, 2024). Policy-oriented evidence also points to persistent labor and skills shortages in the agro-food sector and highlights training and automation as key responses, which aligns with viewing labor-efficiency as an investable lever (Ryan, 2023). From an optimization perspective, recent network models explicitly determine optimal investments in labor productivity across supply-chain activities, strengthening the methodological foundation for incorporating labor-efficiency investment into supply-chain decision frameworks (Nagurney, 2022).
Nevertheless, existing work rarely embeds labor-efficiency investment within a multi-actor strategic setting where low-carbon policy pressure and market signals jointly shape dynamic adjustments, an issue we address in our evolutionary-game framework. Accordingly, in this study, labor-efficiency investment is framed as a quality and loss-control effort at the exporter level, rather than an explicit emission-reduction technology.
2.3 Consumer low-carbon preference and labeling effect in the low-carbon agricultural supply chain
Carbon product certifications and eco-labels have become central instruments for translating consumers' low-carbon preferences into market signals in agri-food systems. Rather than operating as a one-way demand shifter, labeling often induces a bidirectional interaction: labels shape consumer choices by reducing information asymmetry and enhancing perceived credibility, while consumers' low-carbon demand feeds back into firms' incentives to expand certified supply and invest in verification and compliance (Felicetti et al., 2024). Recent evidence further suggests that the effectiveness of this “labeling channel” depends on label governance and design. Clear, intuitive formats and credible third-party certification can strengthen consumer responses and help carbon information compete with incumbent food labels (Wang et al., 2026). Certification-system research also highlights that rising demand for eco-friendly food is pushing producers to adopt certification schemes that signal smaller carbon footprints, reinforcing the role of labeling as a coordination interface between consumption preferences and sustainable production (Bartzas et al., 2025).
Empirical studies have begun to quantify how carbon labels affect consumers' willingness to pay and how responses vary across groups and information settings. For instance, a choice-experiment study on carbon-labeled eggs finds positive but heterogeneous willingness to pay, and shows that information interventions about global warming and the meaning of carbon labels can increase consumers' propensity to pay a premium (Liu, 2025). From a systems perspective, feedback-mechanism modeling similarly indicates that increasing uptake of carbon-labeled products can stimulate both demand and producers' low-carbon offerings, generating a self-reinforcing loop of certified supply and demand (Zhao and Zhong, 2015). However, the literature also points to a persistent gap in linking consumer preferences with supply-chain responses: treating supply- and demand-side stages separately can weaken information flows and leave coordination opportunities underexploited (Yang et al., 2023). This motivates a modeling approach that explicitly captures iterative interactions among consumers and supply-chain actors and examines how labeling-mediated preferences translate into dynamic strategic adjustments.
Overall, the evidence suggests that carbon labeling works as a coordination and feedback mechanism in agri-food supply chains, shaping consumer choices while simultaneously restructuring firms' incentives to supply and certify low-carbon products.
2.4 Evolutionary game modeling in the low-carbon agricultural supply chain
Evolutionary game theory (EGT) has become a widely used approach for analyzing dynamic strategic interactions in low-carbon supply chains, particularly when multiple players adjust their behaviors over time under policy constraints and market signals. This is especially relevant for agricultural supply chains, where bounded rationality, heterogeneous participants, and repeated interactions make dynamics more realistic than one-shot optimization.
Recent studies can be organized into three closely related streams. First, EGT has been applied to examine policy-market co-evolution under carbon regulation, showing how incorporating consumer-side responses can materially affect stability and equilibrium outcomes in carbon trading systems (Chen et al., 2025). Second, governance-oriented work uses EGT to model multi-stakeholder supervision and coordination in low-carbon supply chains (Gong et al., 2025). In agricultural product supply chains, collaborative governance frameworks further integrate key players (e.g., enterprises, government, NGOs, and consumers) into a unified evolutionary setting and demonstrate how embedding sustainability and quality-related incentives in payoff structures can promote stable, low-carbon trajectories (Cao and Tao, 2025). Third, agriculture-specific applications increasingly focus on farm-level low-carbon decisions and incentive compatibility: evolutionary models involving government, farmers, and consumers illustrate how regulatory tools and consumer preferences jointly shape low-carbon production choices (Xie et al., 2022), while carbon-trading-based evolutionary analyses of farmer organizations highlight how government interventions and trading incentives influence agricultural emission-reduction behavior and adoption stability (Chu et al., 2025).
The above studies demonstrate that evolutionary game models not only reflect the dynamic interactions among low-carbon agricultural supply chain actors but also allow exploration of how changes in one part of the system propagate through the strategic evolution of the whole supply chain.
2.5 Research gaps and contributions
Existing studies offer valuable insights into low-carbon agricultural supply chains, but important gaps remain. Accordingly, we synthesize the existing literature to identify these gaps and clarify the specific contributions of our study as follows:
(1) Although numerous studies have examined technological investment in the low-carbon agricultural supply chain, most rely on static or one-shot optimization models and do not capture the dynamic adjustment and co-evolution of technological investments over time under changing policy and market signals.
(2) Labor-efficiency investment has been widely explored as a driver of operational performance and waste reduction in perishable agri-food supply chains, yet current research rarely employs multi-player evolutionary game frameworks to model how key players jointly adapt labor-efficiency investments and other related strategies under changing incentives and bounded rationality.
(3) Research on consumer preferences and carbon certification has concentrated on demand-side willingness-to-pay, with limited attention to the two-way feedback between consumer preferences and upstream supply chain decisions.
(4) Research on export-oriented agricultural supply chains has largely remained at the macro level, and even product-specific studies have rarely examined the low-carbon transformation of the China-EU garlic export supply chain under certification and trade-related constraints.
(5) Furthermore, the agricultural sector in both the EU and China is not mandatorily integrated into formal carbon-trading schemes in a uniform manner, but is often encouraged to engage in the carbon-trading schemes such as the China Certified Emission Reduction (CCER) program. Research on agricultural supply chains from a carbon-trading perspective remains scant, especially when combined with certification-driven demand signals.
Compared with existing research, our study integrates these elements into a four-party evolutionary game model of China's garlic export supply chain. The model jointly captures suppliers' technology investment, exporters' labor-efficiency investment, a foreign competitor's strategy, and consumers' low-carbon preferences under EU low-carbon policy constraints. Replicator-dynamics simulations characterize the co-evolution of multiple players and identify conditions for a stable low-carbon, carbon-certified equilibrium.
3 Evolutionary game model composed of four parties
In this research, we examine a four-level supply chain composed of a Chinese Farmer (supplier), a Chinese Exporter (export manufacturer), an EU Farmer (foreign manufacturer), and an EU Consumer (consumer). These entities serve as critical components of the supply chain, each acting in a manner that reflects their inherent risk aversion and a common goal of profit maximization. Within the evolutionary game framework, the decision-making behavior of each participant is shaped by bounded rationality, that is, they cannot always make perfectly informed choices regarding costs and benefits (Tian and Sun, 2022). Instead, they adapt their strategies over time through a process of trial and error, gradually converging toward an optimal or stable decision-making approach.
We model these four parties because they constitute the most influential decision nodes that form a minimal closed-loop feedback in this cross-border agri-food chain. Other players, such as EU importers and retailers, are not introduced as separate strategic populations because their primary roles are intermediation and price pass-through, which are captured in the model through reduced-form trade and pricing terms. Regulators and certification authorities are treated as an exogenous institutional environment, and their impacts enter the payoff structure via policy and compliance parameters rather than endogenous strategies.
While large exporters or EU manufacturers may possess certain forward-looking planning capabilities, the decisions examined here are shaped by repeated interactions under evolving policy constraints, strategy decisions, and implementation limits across the supply chain. Therefore, evolutionary game theory is adopted to capture adaptive learning and gradual strategy revision at the population level, rather than one-shot fully informed optimization.
3.1 Model assumptions
This section presents an explanation of the problem in our model, and a summary of the relevant variables and notation is provided in Table 1.
Table 1
| Parameters | |
|---|---|
| Cs | Unit production cost of the supplier |
| Ct | Unit cost of suppliers' carbon emission reduction |
| Cm | Unit production cost of the export manufacturer |
| Ca | Unit production cost of the foreign manufacturer |
| Ps0 | Price of normal products sold by the supplier |
| Ps1 | Price of carbon-certified products sold by the supplier |
| Pm0 | Price of normal products sold by the export manufacturer |
| Pm1 | Price of carbon-certified products sold by the export manufacturer |
| Pam0 | Price of normal products sold by a foreign manufacturer |
| Pam1 | Price of carbon-certified products sold by a foreign manufacturer |
| Vc | Low-carbon technologies investment cost of the supplier |
| Vl | Labor-efficiency investment cost of the export manufacturer |
| Vca | Low-carbon technology investment cost of a foreign manufacturer |

The game model includes four parties that form a typical supply chain network, and we have the following assumptions:
Assumption 1 (game players):The four-party game comprises a Chinese Farmer, aChinese Exporter, an EU Farmer, and an EU Consumer.
To model the bounded rational strategic adjustment in this supply chain, we define the strategy sets of the four players as follows:
Assumption 2 (strategies of game players):Each player has two available strategies.The Chinese Farmer chooses whether to invest in low-carbon technologies; the ChineseExporter chooses whether to implement labor-efficiency investment; the EU Farmerchooses whether to invest in low-carbon technologies; and the EU Consumer chooseswhether to purchase carbon-certified products.
Let x ∈ [0, 1] denote the probability that the Chinese Farmer chooses to invest in low-carbon technologies. Then, the probability that the Chinese Farmer does not choose to invest in low-carbon technologies is 1 − x. Let y ∈ [0, 1] denote the probability that the Chinese Exporter chooses to implement labor-efficiency investment. Then, the probability that the Chinese Exporter does not choose to implement labor-efficiency investment is 1 − y. Let s ∈ [0, 1] denote the probability that the EU Farmer chooses to invest in low-carbon technologies. Then, the probability that the EU Farmer does not choose to invest in low-carbon technologies is 1 − s. Let z ∈ [0, 1] denote the probability that the EU Consumer chooses to buy carbon-certified products. Then, the probability that the EU Consumer does not choose to buy carbon-certified products is 1 − z. And more, x, y, s, and z are functions of time t. This depicts the phenomenon of probability distribution changing over time. In summary, we have the following assumption:
Assumption 3 (strategy distribution)The four players in the game randomly selectfrom their strategy sets, forming a four-dimensional simplex.
Here, the cost items of Chinese Farmer include the investment cost of low-carbon technologies, the unit production cost of garlic products, and the carbon emission cost of garlic cultivation. The investment cost of low-carbon technologies is denoted by Vc. The unit production cost of garlic products is denoted by Cs.
If the Chinese Farmer does not invest in low-carbon technologies, then their carbon emission cost is denoted by Ct, otherwise, their carbon emission cost is denoted by μCt. Here, με(0, 1) Here, represents the cost adjustment parameter after the Chinese Farmer invests in low-carbon technologies, reducing the overall carbon emissions.
If the Chinese Farmer invests in low-carbon technologies, then the transaction price between the Chinese Farmer and the Chinese Exporter is denoted by Ps1, otherwise, the transaction price is denoted by Ps0. Here, Ps1 > Ps0.
In summary, we have the following assumption:
Assumption 4 (production costs and sale prices of the Chinese Farmer):The ChineseFarmer's garlic cultivation involves costs for low-carbon-technology investment, unitproduction, and carbon emissions, with emission costs reduced by an adjustmentparameter when investment occurs. Transaction prices are higher under investment andlower otherwise.
The Chinese Exporter's unit cost of production is Cm. The Chinese Exporter's cost associated with implementing labor-efficiency investment is . This labor-efficiency investment is primarily an operational measure to improve product quality and reduce perishability during long-distance transport; it does not represent a direct carbon-abatement action in our model, although lower spoilage may indirectly reduce waste-related embodied emissions per effectively delivered unit. Without the investment, the price at which the Chinese Exporter sells the product is Pm0; and is the adjusted price that the manufacturer implements the investment, whereas Pm1 > Pm0.
The quality enhancement coefficient is introduced to capture the effect of labor-efficiency investment on product quality and perishability, while Qm > 1. And when there is no labor-efficiency investment. When the Chinese exporter markets its products to EU consumers, it incurs a suite of costs, including EU-imposed agricultural tariffs, vehicle and vessel taxes during transit, insurance premiums, and the like. We define , the comprehensive export coefficient is the aggregate ratio of these costs to the goods' total value. Economically, τ is an ad valorem trade-cost wedge aggregating tariffs, border charges, and international logistics costs; the baseline calibration is provided in the Supplementary material.
In summary, we have the following assumption:
Assumption 5 (production costs and sale prices of the Chinese Exporter):TheChinese Exporter's choice of whether to invest in labor-efficiency technologiesinvolves significant differences in export garlic production quality and marketshare.
The EU Farmer competes with the Chinese exporter in the EU market and is characterized by a side-specific cost-price structure that differs from that of the Chinese Farmer. Accordingly, the EU Farmer's unit production cost is denoted as Ca. Additionally, producing carbon-certified products incurs an extra cost Vca, reflecting the investment required for low-carbon technologies and certifications. The selling price of foreign manufacturers' carbon-certified products is Pam1, where the normal product's price is Pam0, where Pam1 > Pm1 > Pam0 > Pm0. This asymmetry also reflects different policy and certification exposure across the two sides: cross-border compliance for the export chain vs. domestic compliance for the EU competitor, which is captured through terms in the payoff structure.
In summary, we have the following assumption:
Assumption 6 (production costs and sale prices of the EU Farmer):The EU Farmer'schoice of whether to invest in low-carbon technologies involves significant differences ingarlic production costs and sales prices.
The EU Consumer's perceived value for each product type is determined by the values v1 and v0. In the case where carbon-certified products are not available, the consumer is forced to purchase non-low-carbon products, resulting in a passive loss l0 associated with their choice. Similarly, when carbon-certified products are unavailable, but the consumer is forced to purchase them due to their preference for sustainability, they experience a passive loss l1, representing the difference between their ideal product and the one they are compelled to buy. Here, l0 and l1 are modeled on the same scale as consumers' perceived values v0 and v1, capturing the utility loss from preference mismatch.
It is important to note that the parameters l0 and l1 are only meaningful under the premise that consumers have an intrinsic preference for carbon-certified products. Therefore, these parameters are not freely adjustable across their full theoretical domains. In the context of this study, we impose a contextual restriction that l0 and l1 must be sufficiently positive to reflect the tension between low-carbon demand and conventional supply. In our parameterization, we restrict l0, l1 ≥ 0, to ensure economically meaningful preference-mismatch penalties.
In summary, we have the following assumption:
Assumption 7 (production costs and sale prices of the EU Consumer):The EUConsumer's choice of whether to purchase carbon-certified garlic involves significantdifferences in perceived value and passive loss.
The demand market is denoted as D. The market is characterized by a preference differential between Chinese and EU products. This is represented by the parameters θD and (1 − θ)D, where θ reflects the market share of Chinese export products and 1 − θ corresponds to the market share of local products. Moreover, the demand for Chinese export products is influenced by the quality improvement coefficient Qm, which is assumed to impact the market share of these products. Specifically, the market share of Chinese exports and local products becomes θQm and 1 − θQm. To ensure the feasibility of market shares, we restrict Qm such that 0 ≤ θQm ≤ 1. Economically, a higher Qm reflects improved export quality and lower spoilage, which increases the relative attractiveness of Chinese exports and shifts demand shares accordingly.
When the product type does not match the consumer's preference, the Chinese Exporter and EU Farmer will apply price discounts. The discount coefficient δ represent price reduction factors for the Chinese Exporter and the EU Farmer, respectively. For the Chinese Exporter, actual selling prices are adjusted to δPm1 for carbon-certified products and δPm0 for normal products. Similarly, the EU farmers' prices are adjusted to δPam1 and δPam0. This mechanism reflects manufacturers' response to consumer preferences shifts. For simplicity and tractability, we use a common δ for both sellers as an exogenous discount factor; heterogeneity in discounting can be explored in sensitivity analysis.
In summary, we have the following assumption:
Assumption 8 (coefficients of quality enhancement, market share, and discount):The effects of labor-efficiency investment are summarized by two positive coefficients: aquality enhancement coefficient and a market-share sensitivity coefficient. The effect of EUconsumers' preferences is summarized by a discount-pass-through coefficient fromwholesale to retail prices.

5.3 Sensitivity analysis on key parameters
5.3.1 Effect of the Chinese Farmer's investment cost
To examine how the export manufacturer's labor-efficiency investment cost affects the evolutionary outcomes, we assign Vl = {0.08, 0.10, 0.12, 0.14, 0.16} and simulate the replicator dynamics under the baseline parameters of Table 8. The resulting strategy trajectories are plotted in Figure 6, where each curve corresponds to one of the five Vl levels, and all four strategy shares start from the initial proportions of 0.25.
Figure 6
In Figure 6, the supplier's low-carbon technology investment strategy share rises from its initial value to 1 in every case, confirming that the supplier ultimately chooses to implement low-carbon technology investment. The time required to reach equilibrium stays almost stable as Vl grows, indicating that labor-efficiency investment costs have little influence on the supplier's strategy.
In terms of the export manufacturer's labor-efficiency investment share, all curves converge to y=1, i.e. “implement labor-efficiency investment.” Yet, as Vl increases, the time required to reach equilibrium increases, which shows that the cost is the critical factor that influences export manufacturers' labor-efficiency investment strategy.
By contrast, the foreign manufacturer's low-carbon technology investment strategy share remains virtually unaffected by Vl in every simulation, s quickly climbs to 1 and stabilizes, reflecting that foreign-side incentives are decoupled from the export manufacturer's labor-cost parameter.
The consumer's strategy of pursuing low-carbon certified products exhibits a clear delay when Vl increases. All curves eventually jump from near zero to 1, indicating consumers switch to pursue low-carbon certified products with a fluctuation. However, the higher the Vl, the later this jump occurs. For example, with Vl=0.08, z reaches equilibrium by about t ≈ 100, whereas for Vl=0.16 it only does so near t ≈ 200.
These results can be explained by the model's dual-mechanism structure. A larger Vl raises the export manufacturer's cost of labor-efficiency investment, which both delays its own strategy change and weakens the downstream quality signal that drives consumer adoption. Consequently, consumers postpone their switch to low-carbon certified products.

5.3.2 Effect of EU tariff rates on garlic

Figure 9
As shown in Figure 9, the supplier's share x(t) converges rapidly to unity in every case, and the convergence speed is only marginally affected by the tariff level, indicating that the supplier's decision to invest in low-carbon technology remains robust across a wide range of import duties. In Figure 9, the export manufacturer's share y(t) likewise rises to 1 in all simulations, but higher tariff rates accelerate this convergence: as τ increases, the export manufacturer more quickly commits to labor-efficiency investment.
By contrast, the foreign manufacturer's share s(t) is essentially insensitive to changes in τ, converging nearly instantaneously to full low-carbon investment regardless of the import duty. This reflects the foreign manufacturer's strategic independence from the tariff applied to export-oriented products. The consumer low-carbon preference share z(t) exhibits a non-monotonic response: initially, higher tariffs, by raising the price of imported low-carbon certified products, spur consumers to switch to low-carbon certified products more quickly, but once the import price exceeds that of local low-carbon alternatives, the decision speed slows markedly and may even reverse, with consumers ultimately opting for normal products despite the continued availability of local green options.
5.3.3 Effect of the discount coefficient
Figure 10 illustrates the evolutionary responses of each party to variations in the discount coefficient δ = {0.86, 0.88, 0.90, 0.92, 0.94}, with all strategy shares initialized at 0.25.
Figure 10
In Figure 10, the supplier's low-carbon technology investment share x(t) converges to unity at essentially the same rate for all values of δ. This invariance indicates that the supplier's decision to adopt low-carbon technology is governed primarily by carbon-related costs rather than by price discounts on products.
The export manufacturer's labor-efficiency investment share y(t) rises more rapidly as δ increases. When the discount coefficient is low (δ = 0.86), the manufacturer's shift to efficiency upgrades is comparatively gradual; at higher δ values, the convergence curves move leftward, signaling faster adoption.
The foreign manufacturer's low-carbon technology investment share s(t) displays pronounced oscillations for lower δ but rapidly stabilizes at unity as δ grows. Smaller discounts lead to greater early-stage volatility in green-investment decisions, whereas deeper discounts dampen these fluctuations and speed convergence.
Finally, the consumer's low-carbon preference share z(t) remains fluctuating between 0.4 and 0 for an extended period when δ is small, then abruptly jumps to one. As δ increases, this jump occurs earlier and with fewer pre-transition oscillations, indicating that stronger price discounts on normal products initially discourage consumer switch to low-carbon certified goods.
Together, these dynamics underscore a critical feedback loop in which normal product pricing influences both the timing of midstream efficiency investments and the downstream adoption of green products. In particular, the export manufacturer's accelerated investment in labor-efficiency under larger discounts directly facilitates and is reinforced by the consumer's subsequent shift to low-carbon certified purchases.

To examine the effect of the domestic export market share on strategic evolution, we assign θ = {0.15, 0.30, 0.45, 0.60, 0.75} and simulate the replicator dynamics under the same baseline parameters, initializing each strategy share at 0.25.
The market-share coefficient θ exerts a clear influence on the speed with which each party adopts its strategy. In Figure 11, the supplier's low-carbon technology investment share x(t) converges to one in every simulation. As θ increases from 0.15 to 0.75, the supplier reaches full adoption slightly faster, reflecting the fact that a larger export market share improves the payoff of low-carbon technology investment and thus accelerates the supplier's strategic shift.

Likewise, the export manufacturer's labor-efficiency investment share y(t) climbs from its initial value to unity for all θ levels. Higher values of θ bring the convergence curves leftward, so that a manufacturer with a larger export market share adopts efficiency improvements more quickly. This trend highlights how midstream firms respond to market-size incentives: the greater the proportion of domestic exports, the stronger the incentive to upgrade production processes.
The foreign manufacturer's low-carbon technology investment share s(t) exhibits non-monotonic dynamics. When θ is low at 0.15, s(t) converges rapidly to one with minimal oscillation, as the foreign player retains a substantial market share. At moderate θ values, which are 0.45 and 0.60, s(t) undergoes pronounced oscillations before stabilizing at unity, indicating that an intermediate foreign-market share creates competing pressures on green adoption. Interestingly, when θ reaches 0.75, the foreign manufacturer again converges swiftly, suggesting that a very small foreign share compels a rapid green-technology pivot to remain competitive in a niche market.
The consumer green-preference share z(t) remains near zero until a threshold time, then jumps sharply to one. As θ increases, this jump occurs earlier and with fewer oscillations, demonstrating that greater export availability of certified products facilitates consumer uptake. However, for θ between 0.45 and 0.75, further increases in the foreign-import share actually slow the consumers' transition to low-carbon choices. In other words, even though imported low-carbon products may hold a price advantage, market share alone does not determine consumers' green adoption speed.
These dynamics illustrate that shifts in export market share not only influence producers' decisions to invest in low-carbon and efficiency technologies but also interact with consumer preferences in a non-linear fashion, underscoring the complexity of coordinating upstream and downstream strategies in export-oriented supply chains.
5.3.5 Effect of the carbon-emission reduction coefficient on the evolutionary game
As a final parameter of interest, we examine the carbon-emission reduction efficiency μ by assigning μ = {0.80, 0.82, 0.84, 0.86, 0.88}, with all strategy shares initialized at 0.25. The resulting trajectories are plotted in Figure 12.
Figure 12
In Figure 12, the supplier's low-carbon technology investment share x(t) still rises toward one, but the convergence time lengthens as μ increases. A higher μ implies a lower emission reduction per unit of investment, thereby diminishing the incentive for low-carbon technology adoption. When μ reaches a critical level (e.g., 0.88), x(t) even falls back toward zero, indicating that the supplier ultimately abandons its low-carbon investment under insufficient reduction effects.
The export manufacturer's labor-efficiency investment share y(t) converges to unity in every case, yet the time to reach y = 1 grows longer as μ increases. This slower adjustment arises because reduced emission-reduction benefits weaken the manufacturer's justification for efficiency upgrades.
By contrast, the foreign manufacturer's s(t) is largely insensitive to μ: all curves quickly jump to one with minimal variation, demonstrating that this party's decision depends chiefly on export market incentives rather than the domestic carbon reduction parameter.
The consumer green-preference share z(t) likewise shows delayed convergence as μ increases. The curves rise from zero to one after a threshold time, and larger μ values postpone this transition. Notably, at μ = 0.88, when domestic suppliers have ceased low-carbon production, European consumers still opt for normal products despite the availability of local green alternatives. This counterintuitive outcome highlights that, for Chinese garlic exports to Europe, price advantage alone does not guarantee consumer green adoption; the upstream supply chain's own commitment to low-carbon production also profoundly shapes downstream preferences.
Together, these results illustrate that the emission-reduction efficiency parameter μ critically governs the pace, and in extreme cases, the direction of strategic evolution for both producers and consumers, underscoring the need for sufficiently effective carbon technologies to sustain coordinated low-carbon transitions.

5.4 Result discussion and implication
The evolutionary game analysis above reveals multiple possible long-run strategic outcomes. The stability analysis identifies all 16 pure-strategy combinations, but only four emerge as evolutionarily stable strategies (ESS) under realistic parameter conditions, which we interpret through mechanisms and implications below.
5.4.1 Key findings and mechanism interpretation
In this evolutionary system, the four players are tightly interconnected, with each party's decisions exerting mutual influence. Our analysis identifies four pure-strategy equilibria, among which the ideal equilibrium is (1,1,1,1). The fully low-carbon certified outcome becomes attainable when the supplier's low-carbon technology investment and the exporter's labor-efficiency measures reach a sufficiently mature level, such that their costs are relatively low compared to the associated benefits; otherwise, the system may converge to a partially green equilibrium, implying that phased low-carbon transitions remain feasible even when full-chain certification is temporarily out of reach. This finding provides a mechanism-based explanation for why “full-chain” outcomes may not be observed in practice even when individual actors show willingness to upgrade, because stability requires a consistent payoff advantage across all players.
Second, the simulations reveal pronounced non-linear tipping-point behaviors. Small changes in key parameters such as the exporter's investment costs, the EU Farmer's certification cost, tariffs, and market-share dynamics can shift the system from one equilibrium to another. In particular, modest cost reductions in labor-efficiency investment may hasten consumer acceptance of certified low-carbon products, while increased certification difficulty for the foreign competitor can create a critical tipping point that redirects consumer choices toward Chinese certified garlic, thereby reinforcing upstream incentives to remain green. These results indicate that policy and market forces may trigger abrupt strategy shifts once critical incentive thresholds are crossed, rather than producing smooth linear adjustments.
Beyond producer and policy side parameters, incorporating consumer perceived value and loss dynamics adds an additional layer of strategic complexity. A larger passive purchase loss l1 delays consumers' transition toward proactive low-carbon purchasing, yet it can accelerate the timing of investment responses by producers, and similar effects are observed for l0 under additional equilibrium conditions. Moreover, allowing perceived values to vary across consumer segments yields fundamentally different stability landscapes. Overall, once consumer–producer interactions are accounted for, the evolutionary trajectory and the feasibility of achieving a fully low-carbon, export-oriented certified garlic chain become more complex than a producer-only perspective would suggest. This highlights that consumer-side frictions and heterogeneity can be “binding constraints” on certification transitions, even when supply-side upgrading is economically plausible.
5.4.2 Policy implications
The existence of multiple ESS and threshold-driven transitions suggests that policy design should account for discontinuities in behavioral responses. In practice, interventions may have limited effect until incentives reach a minimum effective intensity; thus, targeted packages that reduce key adoption costs and strengthen credible demand-side signals are more likely to push the system across critical tipping points. In the EU policy context, trade measures and low-carbon requirements should be assessed jointly as a combined incentive environment, because their interaction can determine whether the system transitions to a fully low-carbon equilibrium or remains locked in a partly green regime. Since fully low-carbon outcomes depend on the weakest link in the chain, policy support that prioritizes the bottleneck actor can facilitate phased transitions toward full-chain certification.
5.4.3 Managerial implications
Our results suggest that low-carbon upgrading in export-oriented perishable supply chains works better as a planned sequence with basic coordination, rather than isolated moves by individual players. For farmers, the key managerial question is when to invest in low-carbon technologies and documentation: the model indicates that early adoption is more likely to be sustained when the expected certification premium and compliance pressure are meaningful; otherwise, the system may settle into a partially green outcome. For exporters, labor-efficiency investment should be treated as an operational decision aimed at protecting delivered quality, packaging standards, shelf-life, and market share under long-distance logistics; when perishability risk is high, prioritizing these measures helps keep certified products commercially viable.
The simulations also show threshold effects: small, incremental actions may not shift market outcomes until a critical point is reached. This calls for a phased certification strategy—start with pilot certification and scale up once demand response becomes visible—rather than an all-at-once transition. To make such sequencing work, exporters and farmers should adopt simple coordination mechanisms (e.g., sharing certification, traceability costs, longer-term contracting, and joint quality-related investment) so that the party bearing upgrade costs is aligned with the party capturing downstream price premia. Also, exporters can speed up consumer acceptance by reducing purchase frictions through verifiable certification and transparent carbon information, which improves the stability of low-carbon outcomes.
At the same time, the results should be interpreted within the model's boundary conditions, such as parameterization and stylized behavioral assumptions; future research may calibrate key parameters using empirical or industry data and extend the framework to richer market structures and heterogeneous consumer segments.

6 Conclusion
China's garlic exports to the EU have surged in recent years, bridging seasonal production gaps between the two regions. At the same time, both China and the EU have encouraged voluntary agricultural carbon-reduction certification, while the EU has rolled out the related policies to foster sustainable, low-carbon farming practices. As of June 2025, de-globalization trends and escalating tariff conflicts continue to reshape international agricultural trade. Against this backdrop, and noting that most Chinese exports remain unlabeled, raw garlic, the opportunity for an export-oriented, carbon-certified garlic supply chain represents a true blue-ocean market. Garlic is used as a representative export-oriented perishable agri-food product characterized by strong competition, certification, and trade-policy constraints, which makes it suitable for illustrating the evolutionary mechanisms studied in this paper. To explore this potential, we develop a four-party evolutionary game model. By examining how key parameters influence both stability thresholds and dynamic trajectories, our study offers theoretical foundations and practical guidance for realizing a fully low-carbon, carbon-certified garlic export industry.
It should be noted that the scope of our model is inherently limited to a stylized four-party framework and a specific commodity context. While this allows us to clearly identify fundamental strategic interactions and tipping-point phenomena, caution is warranted when generalizing the quantitative thresholds or assuming homogeneous behavior across different industries. Moreover, our evolutionary game setting adopts bounded rationality and replicator dynamics to represent adaptive learning and gradual strategy revision. While major exporters and EU manufacturers may engage in forward-looking planning, our approach does not explicitly model fully rational intertemporal optimization; rather, it focuses on long-run adaptation under policy uncertainty, strategy decisions, and adjustment constraints. Future research may compare our evolutionary outcomes with forward-looking dynamic-game or intertemporal optimization formulations to assess how alternative behavioral assumptions affect equilibrium selection and transition paths.
In addition, consumer perceived values and passive-purchase loss parameters are treated as fixed within the baseline replicator system, which provides tractability but may abstract from heterogeneity across consumer segments. Extending the model to incorporate segmented consumers and distributional preference parameters would be a promising direction for future work.
Finally, EU policy and market pressures in our setting mainly work by inducing Chinese supply-chain actors to invest in abatement and obtain credible carbon-footprint certification. Future research could map a timeline of key EU import-related policy developments and connect major policy shifts to specific garlic trade routes and stages of the trade lifecycle, while also improving parameterization by quantifying emission sources across production and cold-chain logistics. Moreover, voluntary carbon-credit mechanisms (e.g., CCER-type schemes) and regulatory interventions may be incorporated to assess how policy designs shape strategic interactions and progress toward carbon neutrality. Nevertheless, our insights offer useful guidance for sustainable agri-food supply chains.

articles.title: Carbon Credit Validation, Verification, and Certification Market Forecast to 2030: Industry is Poised for Expansion, Particularly in Agriculture, Forestry, and Industrial Manufacturing Sectors
articles.author: GlobeNewswire
articles.content:
Dublin, April 13, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- The "Carbon Credit Validation, Verification, and Certification Market by Type, Service, Application & Region - Global Forecast to 2030" has been added to ResearchAndMarkets.com's offering.
The global carbon credit validation, verification, and certification market is predicted to surge to USD 448.0 million by 2030 from USD 161.6 million in 2025, marking a CAGR of 22.6%. This positive outlook is significantly driven by increasing regulatory pressures and a rise in corporate and public consciousness about climate change.
The compliance segment is expected to be the second-largest market from 2025 to 2030. Compliance frameworks such as the EU ETS and California's Cap-and-Trade Program drive the demand for verified carbon credits to meet regulatory demands, fostering investment in validation processes that uphold the credibility and standards of carbon credits.
Prominent players include VERRA (US), Gold Standard (Switzerland), ACR (US), Climate Action Reserve (US), SGS (Switzerland), DNV GL (Norway), TUV SUD (Germany), Intertek Group plc (UK), and Bureau Veritas (France), among others. These companies are central to maintaining the integrity of the carbon credit market, fostering innovation, and driving market growth.
Governments globally continue to enforce stricter carbon-reduction regulations, and more companies are adopting net-zero targets, leading to an escalated demand for verified carbon credits. This heightened demand is paving the way for technological innovations, notably in remote sensing, GIS, and blockchain, which are set to boost the efficiency of validation and verification processes.
With the growth of compliance and voluntary carbon markets, the industry is poised for expansion, particularly in agriculture, forestry, and industrial manufacturing sectors. This growth not only promises new revenue streams but also underscores the crucial role of businesses in validating carbon credits, thereby aiding in global climate change mitigation efforts.
Industrial Segment Prospects:
The industrial sector is projected to hold the third-largest market share in 2024. Industries like cement, steel, and chemicals are significant greenhouse gas emitters, heightening the need for independent assurance services to verify and monetize emission reductions. Regulatory mandates and corporate sustainability commitments drive the industrial sector to seek third-party validation for carbon credit generation and compliance.
Market Developments and Diversification:
- Drivers: Increasing carbon credit scrutiny, expanded climate disclosure, demand from legacy projects.
- Restraints: Decline in new project registrations, cost sensitivity, global regulatory uncertainty.
- Opportunities: Article 6 mechanisms, growth in nature-based projects, digital MRV technologies.
- Challenges: Reputational risks from low-quality projects, capacity constraints, market fragmentation.

articles.title: SSE and TotalEnergies UK Wind Farm Delays Contract That Would Cap Profits
articles.author: Bloomberg.com
articles.content:
One of the UK’s largest offshore wind farms delayed starting a government contract that would cap the price of its electricity, instead choosing to sell power in the market at more profitable rates.
The Seagreen wind farm, whose owners include SSE Plc and TotalEnergies SE, expects to delay one of its fixed-price contracts until the fall, rather than starting at the end of March, according to data compiled by Bloomberg from the government-owned company that runs the subsidy mechanism. The contract represents about 13% of the capacity of the wind farm off Scotland’s east coast.

articles.title: New degree option and courses launched in service systems engineering
articles.author: Penn State Engineering News
articles.content:
Penn State's Harold and Inge Marcus Department of Industrial and Manufacturing Engineering has established new curricula for students interested in learning about or working in the service sector. Credit: Credit: iStock/serts
New degree option and courses launched in service systems engineering
Apr 24, 2026
By Emily Liu
UNIVERSITY PARK, Pa. — Penn State’s Harold and Inge Marcus Department of Industrial and Manufacturing Engineering (IME) has launched new curricula for students interested in the service sector. These include a specialized service systems engineering (SSE) option for the bachelor of science degree program in industrial engineering, as well as several new courses on subjects ranging from healthcare systems modeling to pricing and demand management.
"As service industries become more digital, data-rich and AI-enabled, students need more than a traditional view of industrial engineering,” said Vittaldas Prabhu, professor and Charles and Enid Schneider Faculty Chair in Service Enterprise Engineering. “The SSE option gives them a rigorous way to work at the intersection of physical operations, digital platforms and cyber-physical service systems, opening pathways to high-impact careers across healthcare, logistics, consulting, finance and other service sectors.”
Service systems engineering is an area of industrial engineering focused on the development of systems that enhance quality and productivity in the service sector. These systems are continuously redesigned to anticipate real-world fluctuations, saving time and resources for both companies and consumers — for example, by reducing wait times in drive-through lines or improving the efficiency of snow removal.
To help students address modern challenges in service industries, IME has established an SSE option for the bachelor of science degree program in industrial engineering. While the general option for the bachelor's degree provides a well-rounded industrial engineering curriculum, the SSE option provides a specialized curriculum in service systems engineering.
The general option is offered at the University Park and Behrend campuses. The SSE option is exclusively offered at the UP campus.
“The new option provides a distinctive academic path for students interested in service sectors such as healthcare, consulting, digital platforms, supply chains, finance and hospitality,” said chair of the SSE Advisory Board Charles “Chuck” Schneider, a 1962 Penn State alumnus who played a pivotal role in establishing, developing and expanding Penn State’s offerings for service enterprise engineering. “IME is responding to the modern economy with a pathway that is technically rigorous, career-relevant and clearly differentiated.”
In addition to the SSE degree option, IME will offer new courses on service systems engineering starting in the fall semester of the 2026-27 academic year. The new courses are listed with brief descriptions below.
- Introduction to Service Systems Engineering (IE 304): This course provides an introduction to service systems engineering. Students will map service systems, interpret dashboards and telemetry, analyze performance and work in teams on a redesign project, building practical skills for internships and careers.
- Human Systems Networks (IE 427): This course discusses the role of humans in systems of people and things. Students will learn the fundamentals of social network analysis methods, including collecting data from humans in systems and representing behavior and performance in different work domains.
- Introduction to Healthcare Systems Modeling (IE 432): This course prepares students to address challenges specific to the healthcare sector. Key concepts include the structure and operation of healthcare systems, the factors driving decision-making and the application of modeling techniques to health policy.
- Pricing and Demand Management (IE 435): This course provides an overview on ways to improve profitability for organizations in a variety of service industries, covering concepts such as customer demand and choice, traditional and dynamic pricing methods, auction methods and service charges.
- Modeling and Optimization of Stochastic Service Systems (IE 475): This course covers the modeling and evaluation of service systems in practice. Students will learn to simulate and analyze arrival processes, in addition to learning about data-driven approaches for uncertainty modeling, scheduling and optimization.
These courses are open to all interested students who meet the prerequisites for enrollment, including those pursuing the SSE option within the bachelor of science degree program in industrial engineering.
“The service sector represents the majority of the U.S. economy and workforce,” said Ling Rothrock, interim department head and professor of industrial and manufacturing engineering. “Focused coursework in service systems engineering will prepare students to work in a sector with an exciting future that will impact all of us daily.”
Students can email undergrad@ime.psu.edu to learn more.
articles.summary: Penn State's Harold and Inge Marcus Department of Industrial and Manufacturing Engineering has established new curricula for students interested in learning about or working in the service sector. articles.title: SSE and Centrica hit as Reeves threatens to rewire energy pricing
articles.author: Yahoo Finance UK
articles.content:
Shares in SSE PLC (LSE:SSE) and Centrica PLC (LSE:CNA) took a heavy beating on Friday after Chancellor Rachel Reeves signalled that the government is actively working to sever the link between electricity and gas prices - a reform that could fundamentally reshape the economics of the UK energy sector.
SSE fell 5.2% and Centrica dropped 4.9%, making the two utilities among the biggest fallers on the FTSE 100 on a day when the broader mood across European markets was broadly positive, buoyed by hopes of progress in Middle East peace talks.
The sell-off was triggered by comments Reeves made in Washington, where she confirmed that she and Energy Secretary Ed Miliband were working on a "practical way" to delink electricity and gas prices.
Under the UK's current marginal cost pricing model, gas-fired power stations typically set the wholesale price of electricity for the entire market.
The result is that when gas prices rise, consumers pay more across the board - even for electricity generated from wind, solar or nuclear, where production costs are largely unaffected by gas market movements.
Reeves described the proposed reform as "quite a big change" but insisted it was "absolutely the right thing to do," particularly as electricity makes up an increasingly large share of the UK's overall energy mix. She suggested further details could emerge within days or weeks.
Both SSE and Centrica have benefited from the existing pricing structure during periods of elevated gas prices, and any move to decouple the two could compress margins and reduce revenue predictability.
"Whilst the mood seems broadly risk-on on hopes for peace early Friday, with European markets broadly higher and US futures higher, the FTSE 100 dipped as utilities were hit by comments from Chancellor Rachel Reeves about decoupling energy pricing from gas prices," commented Saxo UK investor strategist Neil Wilson.
"Centrica and SSE almost 5% lower each after she said the UK government would look at ending the marginal pricing system that creates higher energy bills for customers than in other countries."

articles.title: SSE and Centrica lifted as UK moves wind and solar farms to fixed-price contracts
articles.author: Proactive financial news
articles.content:
SSE and Centrica lifted as UK moves wind and solar farms to fixed-price contracts
Last updated: 09:46 21 Apr 2026 EDT, First published: 08:35 21 Apr 2026 EDT
Shares in SSE PLC (LSE:SSE), Centrica and several renewable energy investment companies rose after the UK government confirmed plans to move older wind and solar farms onto fixed-price contracts, or else be hit with higher windfall taxes.
SSE, which owns windfarms and hydroelectric power plants, saw its share climb 3.3% to 2,610p on Tuesday, while fellow FTSE 100-listed energy producer Centrica PLC (LSE:CNA), which owns British Gas, and FTSE 250-listed biomass burner Drax Group (LSE:DRX) were up 2.3% and 1.8%.
Specialist investment trusts Bluefield Solar Income Fund Ltd (LSE:BSIF, FRA:5B3), The Renewables Infrastructure Group Limited (LSE:TRIG), Foresight Environmental Infrastructure (LSE:FGEN) and Greencoat UK Wind PLC (LSE:UKW, FRA:3GC) all rose between 5.9% and 2.9%.
The government proposals would see wind and solar farms that currently earn market-linked revenues offered contracts that guarantee a set price for electricity, reducing exposure to volatile gas markets.
These 'wholesale contracts for difference’ will be introduced voluntarily later this year, the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ), with an intention to run an allocation process next year.
Wholesale CfD would offer existing eligible generators that are not already contracted under a CfD, such as some older wind and hydro assets owned by SSE and Centrica, the option to accept a fixed price for the electricity they generate. This would mean that both they and consumers are no longer exposed to volatile gas-linked electricity prices.
The move is aimed at breaking the link between electricity prices and gas in the UK, as wholesale power prices are currently set based on the gas price, despite renewables generating a growing share of power.
Energy Secretary Ed Miliband said: "As we face the second fossil fuel shock in less than 5 years, the lesson for our country is clear: The era of fossil fuel security is over, and the era of clean energy security must come of age. That’s why we’re doubling down on clean power, to give our country energy security and bring down bills for good."
Most of SSE’s newer renewable projects are already on fixed-price contracts, but a significant portion of its older assets still sell power at market rates under the Renewables Obligation scheme.
The proposed wholesale CfDs would target these legacy assets, offering more stable revenues but potentially limiting upside during periods of high electricity prices.
Analysts have previously estimated that such reforms could save UK consumers billions each year by reducing exposure to gas-driven price spikes.
To help persuade generators to accept the fixed-price contracts, Miliband is also raising the windfall tax paid by energy generators on excess profits to 55%, up from the previous 45%.
Officials said this move is expected to generate funds to help the government provide support to households with energy bills.
"Instability in the Middle East has shown that Britain’s reliance on international fossil fuel markets leaves families and businesses exposed to volatile gas prices, driving the cost-of-living crisis even though much of the country’s electricity comes from cheaper renewables and nuclear," DESZN said in a joint statement with the Treasury and 10 Downing Street.
"When wars, geopolitical tensions or supply shocks abroad push up global gas prices, electricity bills rise with them, exposing families to crises they have no control over."

articles.title: SSE tipped to be a big winner thanks to UK government's CfD proposals
articles.author: Proactive financial news
articles.content:
SSE tipped to be a big winner thanks to UK government's CfD proposals
Published: 00:36 25 Apr 2026 AEST
Deutsche Bank has lifted its price target for SSE PLC (LSE:SSE) to 2,900p from 2,850p, with the view that the UK government’s proposed Wholesale Contracts for Difference could become a derisking tool for one of the utility’s most exposed earnings streams.
The broker, which also repeated its 'buy' rating, said the new voluntary market mechanism would offer long-term fixed-price contracts to low-carbon generators currently selling power at market prices.
That matters for SSE because part of its wind generation remains exposed to wholesale power prices, creating both earnings volatility and policy risk.
Deutsche analyst James Brand modelled a scenario in which 8TWh of SSE’s market-exposed wind output is converted into Wholesale CfDs at real prices of £40-50/MWh.
“This could lead to near-term earnings downside of 5-8% if adopted early in 2027/28, and 2-5% in 2028/29,” Brand said in a note.
The trade-off, however, is visibility.
Deutsche Bank said the impact could become more neutral, or even positive, by the early 2030s, while materially reducing risk in the largest market-price-exposed part of SSE’s business.
“It could significantly reduce risk at the largest market price exposed part of SSE, and also lower future government policy risk,” Brand added.
Deutsche Bank’s revised target implies around 9% upside for SSE shares.

The trade-off, however, is visibility.
Deutsche Bank said the impact could become more neutral, or even positive, by the early 2030s, while materially reducing risk in the largest market-price-exposed part of SSE’s business.
“It could significantly reduce risk at the largest market price exposed part of SSE, and also lower future government policy risk,” Brand added.
Deutsche Bank’s revised target implies around 9% upside for SSE shares.
articles.summary: SSE tipped to be a big winner thanks to UK government's CfD proposals Published: 15:36 24 Apr 2026 BST Deutsche Bank has lifted its price target for SSE PLC (LSE:SSE) to 2,900p from 2,850p, with the view that the UK government’s proposed Wholesale Contracts for Difference could become a derisking tool for one of the utility’s most exposed earnings streams.
