- RMT foists sellout deal on London Underground workers
- Eddie Dempsey’s “Improved Pay Offer” on London Underground prepares a sellout, as workers push back
- Eddie Dempsey calls for “compromise” in London Underground “peace talks”: Workers must seize the initiative
- London Underground workers launch powerful strikes: “Our safety is not up for grabs any further”
- London Underground strike: No more RMT sellouts, build rank and file committees to unite all Tube workers
- RMT cancels London tube strikes: A far-reaching betrayal in the making
articles.summary: Around 1,800 train drivers are taking part in two days of strike action this week on London Underground against the introduction of a compressed four-day week by Transport for London (TfL), overseen by Labour Mayor Sadiq Khan. The two 24-hour strikes, running from midday Tuesday to Wednesday and Thursday to Friday, are the opening stage of industrial action, with further two-day stoppages scheduled for May and June.

articles.title: When do the London Tube strikes end and what lines are affected?
articles.author: The Independent
articles.content:
London Underground drivers are on their third day of strike action this week, causing significant travel disruption for commuters and visitors to the capital.
The Rail, Maritime and Transport (RMT) union had announced its members will walk out for 24 hours from midday on Tuesday 21 April, and again on Thursday 23 April.
This means the second strike is starting later today and will continue into Friday.
There are additional strikes planned for May and June.
The RMT has accused Transport for London (TfL) of attempting to impose a new four-day working week, with general secretary Eddie Dempsey expressing frustration over the stalled negotiations.
He said: “We have approached negotiations with TfL in good faith throughout this entire process, but despite our best efforts, TfL seem unwilling to make any concessions in a bid to avert strike action.”
Claire Mann, TfL’s chief operating officer, said the proposals for a four-day working week allow the company to “offer train operators an additional day off, whilst at the same time bringing London Underground in line with the working patterns of other train operating companies, improving reliability and flexibility at no additional cost”.
She added: “The changes would be voluntary, there would be no reduction in contractual hours and those who wish to continue a five-day working week pattern would be able to do so.”
TfL has set out what travellers can expect during strike days, with certain lines more affected than others. Here’s what you need to know:
What dates are the Tube strikes?
April
- Tuesday 21 to Wednesday 22 April
- Thursday 23 to Friday 24 April
May
- Tuesday 19 to Wednesday 20 May
- Thursday 21 to Friday 22 May
June
- Tuesday 16 June to Wednesday 17 June
- Thursday 18 June to Friday 19 June
What time will the Tube shut and reopen?
The planned strike action will take significant parts of the network out of action for half of two consecutive days, lasting from midday to midday.
On Tuesdays and Thursdays travellers can expect normal service until mid-morning, when services will begin to ramp down. There will be significant disruption on all lines from midday, and lines that do run will finish early. TfL recommends completing journeys by 8pm.
On Wednesdays and Fridays, Tube services that do run will begin later, with no service expected before 7.30am. There will be significant disruption until midday, when normal service will begin to resume, but with delays very likely.
Which Tube lines will be affected?
TfL says strikes will affect the whole Tube network, but a reduced service will still run on most lines with significant disruption.
However, there will be no service on the:
- Piccadilly and Circle lines
- Metropolitan line between Baker Street and Aldgate
- Central line between White City and Liverpool Street
On Thursday morning the TfL website also showed all lines will be running a special service with a part closure on the Northern line between Camden Town and Kennington .
Elizabeth line, DLR, London Overground, and tram services will be running normally on strike days, but are likely to be very busy.

This means the second strike is starting later today and will continue into Friday. There are additional strikes planned for May and June.

articles.title: TfL HR employee jailed for £650k tax scam using staff data
articles.author: People Management
articles.content:
A Transport for London (TfL) HR employee has been jailed for stealing colleagues’ personal data to submit £650,000 in fraudulent tax rebate claims, in what a judge described as the organisation’s “worst ever” data breach.
Luciana Akanbi used her access to HR systems to obtain sensitive information from 40 colleagues, including passport details, national insurance numbers and bank data.
She and her husband, Femi Akanbi, used the information to set up self-assessments accounts and submit 139 false claims to HMRC between September 2021 and January 2022, using 38 devices.
The court heard the fraud amounted to losses of £433,000 from the public purse. Both were sentenced to three years and nine months' imprisonment at Woolwich Crown Court.
Prosecutor Andrew Evans said the fraud was "sophisticated" and involved “significant planning”. Judge David Miller also said the breach forced TfL to overhaul its systems and damaged employee trust.
Richard Mullings, head of counter fraud and corruption at TfL, said: “We take any cases of fraud extremely seriously and welcome the court’s sentencing of these two individuals.
“We immediately notified the Information Commissioner’s Office and can reassure those working for us that we have since introduced a range of measures to further tighten up access to personal staff data and ensure this cannot happen again.”
‘Position of trust’
Insider fraud is rising. Data from fraud prevention service Cifas shows cases recorded on its insider threat database have increased by 21 per cent since 2024, with most involving misuse of legitimate access.
Naomi Grossman, compliance manager at eLearning provider VinciWorks, said the case demonstrated the risks tied to HR roles.
“HR professionals hold a pretty unique position of trust, and this case highlights the frightening implications of that trust when it is abused,” she added. “HR professionals have direct access to highly sensitive personal and financial information, and this case shows how that level of access, if not properly controlled, can cause real harm to both individuals and the organisation.”
Daniel Callaghan, CEO of background screening firm Veremark, said HR teams should be subject to similar scrutiny as finance functions. “HR have access to all kinds of personal data and access to payroll. Highly valuable personnel data is at all of their fingertips,” he explained.
“Background screening shouldn’t just stop at the point of employment; continuous screening for toxic traits being displayed across social media can minimise the ongoing risk.”
Jim Moore, employee relations partner at Hamilton Nash, said organisations should monitor how data is accessed. “It’s a big red flag if HR staff are accessing records for employees they don't work with, particularly those in different departments or locations. Likewise, downloading large amounts of data without a clear business reason is another warning.”
Moore also urged employers to support whistleblowing. “Businesses need to make sure they have safe and easy ways for colleagues to raise concerns without fear of being seen as troublemakers,” he said.
Legal and accountability
Under the UK’s new ‘failure to prevent fraud’ offence, which came into force in September 2025, companies are now at risk of criminal prosecution if they fail to prevent fraud that benefits them. Large organisations need to demonstrate that they have taken adequate steps to deter fraud committed by employees, agents or other associated persons.
This offence has been introduced as part of the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023. In the TfL case, the individual benefited from the fraud, rather than the organisation.
Under the UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018, employers have an obligation to protect their staff’s personal data, notify the Information Commissioner’s Office and affected employees where there is a real risk to their rights, and take proportionate steps to reduce harm, said Paman Singh, solicitor advocate and partner at Weightmans. This applies even when data breaches are criminal and deliberate.
“In practice, that means clear communication, practical reassurance and support around issues such as identity theft, credit checks and dealings with HMRC,” explained Singh. “Criminal responsibility may rest with the rogue employee, but regulatory accountability does not follow them out of the door.”
Kate Edwards, associate in the commercial and technology team and the data protection team at Birketts, said that, if employee data is stolen, organisations must be open in their response.
“Transparency with the regulator and affected employees is key. Organisations do not want to be thought of as covering up any security failure,” she warned.
“Implementing and communicating changes shows that an organisation takes its data protection obligations seriously, values its staff and is keen to prevent recurrence.”
articles.summary: A Transport for London (TfL) HR employee has been jailed for stealing colleagues’ personal data to submit £650,000 in fraudulent tax rebate claims, in what a judge described as the organisation’s “worst ever” data breach. Luciana Akanbi used her access to HR systems to obtain sensitive information from 40 colleagues, including passport details, national insurance numbers and bank data.

articles.title: Tube strikes 2026: when are they and how long will they go on for?
articles.author: The Times
articles.content:
Two 24-hour long walkouts on the Tube are disrupting journeys across London this week, with the second strike taking place from noon on Thursday to noon on Friday. Disruption is expected to continue into the afternoons and evenings of strike days. This will be the final walkout of the month, although four more are set to take place across May and June.
Some services are still running, and train and bus journeys are largely taking place as normal. TfL has warned passengers that services are likely to be very busy.
The walkouts are part of six 24-hour strikes taking place over three months. The striking drivers are members of the RMT union who are protesting against Transport for London’s (TfL) proposal to compress a normal working week.
The changes, which are voluntary, will mean the drivers will be working four days instead of five but for more hours per day. While Tube drivers who are members of the Aslef union have accepted the proposals, and will continue to work on RMT strike days, TfL expects the disruption to be significant with no service on some lines. Here’s what you can expect.
When are the next Tube strikes?
The RMT union is planning six 24-hour strikes between April and June.
Dates of the next Tube strikes
- Noon, Thursday, April 23 to 11.59am, Friday, April 24
- Noon, Tuesday, May 19 to 11.59am, Wednesday, May 20
- Noon, Thursday, May 21 to 11.59am, Friday, May 22
- Noon, Tuesday, June 16 to 11.59am, Wednesday, June 17
- Noon, Thursday, June 18 to 11.59am, Friday, June 19
TfL has said that on Tuesdays and Thursdays during the strikes, services will run as normal until mid-morning and be reduced from late morning. After midday there will be significant disruption on all lines, which will continue through to the following day. On Wednesdays and Fridays, there will be significant disruption on all lines until midday. Services will recover in the afternoon but some disruption is likely until the evening.
In terms of which lines are affected, TfL said that most will run a reduced service. However, there will be no service at all on the Piccadilly and Circle lines. In addition, there will be no services on the Metropolitan line between Baker Street and Aldgate, and on the Central line between White City and Liverpool Street.
The Elizabeth line, DLR, London Overground and tram services will be running normally on strike days. Buses are running as normally.
Are there any train strikes planned for 2026?
There are currently no train strikes planned for the foreseeable future. However, there might still be engineering work affecting your journey.
Is Eurostar affected by strikes?
Eurostar isn’t affected by Tube or train strikes, although service may be affected by other walkouts, such as those by Eurotunnel staff or French railway operators, so check before you travel.
How to get to London Heathrow if there’s a strike
Heathrow is one of the best-connected airports in the UK and this helps if there’s a strike. There are frequent coach and TfL bus services, including overnight, when the London Underground is down.
The Heathrow Express and the Elizabeth Line offer alternatives to the Piccadilly Line. National Express buses also operate from several London locations to Heathrow. These alternative services are likely to be busier than usual during the strike days, so make sure to leave plenty of time and plan your journey in advance.
How to get to Gatwick if there’s a train strike
Services to Gatwick are only affected by train strikes and not Tube strikes. Sometimes trains run between central London and Gatwick airport on strike days, but they can be busy. They are also slower and may stop at more stations than usual. Check before you travel as the situation can vary depending on who’s striking. National Express coach services are the cheapest alternative and run regularly.
How to get to Stansted if there’s a train strike
Stansted Express services can be affected during train strike days and on the day after. It’s best to check the schedule before you travel. National Express or the Airport Bus Express shuttle service are the best alternatives.
How to get to Luton airport if there’s a train strike
There are sometimes Thameslink services on train strike days, but it’s best to check before you travel. As an alternative, there are coach services to Luton airport from central London, run by National Express and Arriva’s Greenline.
How to get to London City airport if there’s a train strike
The DLR is the best way to reach London City airport. The airport is also served by London buses.
How to get to Manchester airport if there’s a train strike
During previous strikes, there have been limited train services to Manchester airport but these can get busy. There is a good network of regional buses as an alternative, and you can also catch the Stagecoach service from central Manchester, or National Express services from surrounding cities.
How to get to Birmingham airport if there’s a train strike
There may be limited rail services on strike days — expect these to be busy. Birmingham airport is served by National Express and other coach operators.
Can I get a refund if I miss my holiday because of a rail strike?
While rail companies will refund the cost of your train fare, they are not obliged to do anything else. It’s your responsibility to get to the airport in good time.
Some airlines are more lenient than others if you miss your flight. Some will offer to rebook you on to the next available flight for free, for example.
The best thing you can do is have comprehensive travel insurance, which should cover some of your out-of-pocket expenses if you end up having to cancel elements of your plans.
articles.summary: Two 24-hour long walkouts on the Tube are disrupting journeys across London this week, with the second strike taking place from noon on Thursday to noon on Friday. Disruption is expected to continue into the afternoons and evenings of strike days. This will be the final walkout of the month, although four more are set to take place across May and June. Some services are still running, and train and bus journeys are largely taking place as normal.

articles.title: M Group Lands £99m Deal to Keep TfL’s Bridges Standing Strong
articles.author: Safer Highways
articles.content:
Transport for London (TfL) has awarded a major £99.1 million contract to M Group Transport (Rail & Aviation) to maintain vital bridges and civil structures across the capital’s transport network.
The agreement, confirmed earlier this year following a competitive procurement process under the Procurement Act 2023, will run for an initial five-year period from April 2026 to April 2031, with the option to extend the contract through to 2034.
Covering a wide range of essential maintenance activities, the programme is designed to ensure the continued safety and reliability of London’s infrastructure. Work will include applying protective coatings to structures such as steel, concrete and masonry, as well as managing vegetation and carrying out repairs to tunnels, girders and cable-related assets.
Additional responsibilities under the contract include inspection planning, maintenance of cable draw pits, replacement of damaged identification plates, and both routine and reactive repairs. Scheduled interventions will also take place every four years to help maintain long-term asset condition.
TfL highlighted the importance of the contract in safeguarding operations across its network, with the work playing a key role in preventing deterioration and reducing the risk of incidents.
By investing in ongoing maintenance, the deal aims to support the resilience of London’s transport infrastructure—ensuring it remains safe, reliable and fit for the future.
articles.summary: Transport for London (TfL) has awarded a major £99.1 million contract to M Group Transport (Rail & Aviation) to maintain vital bridges and civil structures across the capital’s transport network. The agreement, confirmed earlier this year following a competitive procurement process under the Procurement Act 2023, will run for an initial five-year period from April 2026 to April 2031, with the option to extend the contract through to 2034.

articles.title: Second London Tube strike to begin at midday
articles.author: BBC
articles.content:
Second Tube strike to impact London from midday
The second in a series of 24-hour strikes by London Underground drivers begins at midday on Thursday.
The strike by members of the Rail, Maritime and Transport union (RMT), which represents roughly half of drivers on the Tube network, is expected to cause travel disruption across the capital.
The union is in a dispute with Transport for London (TfL) over changes to the working week and said it was concerned about the safety impact of proposed shifts lengths. It said it had planned four more 24-hour strikes in May and June if the row was not resolved.
TfL said the industrial action was "completely unnecessary" and the proposed working week pattern was optional.
- The industrial action will begin at 12:00 on Thursday and last for 24 hours
- The Piccadilly and Circle lines will be closed entirely
- The Metropolitan line will be closed between Baker Street and Aldgate
- Central line services will not run between White City and Liverpool Street
- Other lines that do run will be offering a significantly reduced service
- Latest status updates here
Why are Tube drivers striking?
The RMT has rejected an offer for Tube drivers to voluntarily work a four-day week.
Under the proposals, most drivers would see their working week reduced from 36 hours to 35 hours, but their salary would remain the same.
The union said it was concerned about shift lengths, unacceptable working time arrangements and the possible impact of fatigue on safety.
The union it wanted a 32-hour week over four days, which would see drivers work three fewer hours each week for the same salary.
RMT official Jared Wood said: "TfL need to come forward with changes to their proposals for this dispute to be resolved."
Claire Mann, TfL's chief operating officer, said the four day week proposal "allows us to offer train operators an additional day off, whilst at the same time bringing London Underground in line with the working patterns of other train operating companies."
She added: "The changes would be voluntary, there would be no reduction in contractual hours and those who wish to continue a five-day working week pattern would be able to do so."
Forthcoming strikes
- 23–24 April (midday Thursday - midday Friday)
- 19–20 May (midday Tuesday - midday Wednesday)
- 21–22 May (midday Thursday - midday Friday)
- 16–17 June (midday Tuesday - midday Wednesday)
- 18–19 June (midday Thursday - midday Friday)

articles.title: London faces more disruption as second 24-hour tube strike begins
articles.author: The Guardian
articles.content:
Commuters in London face another two days of disruption as a second 24-hour tube strike starts from midday on Thursday.
No further talks have taken place to settle the dispute and drivers in the RMT union will continue industrial action against London Underground plans for a voluntary four-day week after the first 24-hour strike from midday on Tuesday.
Services were reduced but not cancelled across most underground lines. Just over half of the capital’s tube drivers are members of the Aslef union, which has welcomed the four-day week plan, and were not on strike.
Early starters had to find alternative transport with services running only from 7.30am on Wednesday, as Transport for London (TfL) tried to limit overall disruption.
Wider congestion and disruption appeared far lower than in last September’s strikes by all RMT workers, with some companies in the capital relaxing rules to allow more working from home, and fine weather encouraging people to switch to cycling or walking.
Some passengers reported quieter trains than usual on lines where services operated well and commuters had not risked the tube, although most still faced long waits and crowded trains.
Santander bike hires were up 60% on Tuesday morning, TfL said, while Voi, one of the operators of e-scooter and ebike rentals in London, said rides were 52% higher than last week, with significant numbers of new users.
TfL said passengers should continue to check before travelling on Thursday, with services set to be reduced across all lines from midday and finishing by 8pm. On Friday morning the first trains will start from 7.30am.
Most of the Piccadilly, Waterloo & City and Circle lines are expected to have no service during strike hours, along with parts of the Metropolitan and Central lines. Other rail services will run, including the London Overground, Elizabeth line and the DLR.
While Aslef and TfL have expressed surprise at the strike action, the RMT said its drivers had concerns about fatigue, and blamed TfL for failing to negotiate.
TfL said its proposals for a four-day working week would bring London Underground in line with the working patterns of other train operating companies, and that drivers who wished to continue a five-day working week pattern would be able to do so.
An RMT spokesperson said the union objected to an “imposed, fake four-day week” and had raised “serious concerns from our members about shift length and resulting fatigue impacting safety”.
They added: “The strikes are going ahead because TfL said they would negotiate on all elements of the proposal and then U-turned, saying to us they would go ahead without any changes to their original proposals.
“We have sought assurances from TfL in writing that our members can stay on their current shift patterns and agreed terms and conditions. TfL have yet to respond to us adequately. So it is therefore not a voluntary scheme and TfL are seeking to impose it on our members.”
However Nick Dent, the director of customer operations for London Underground, said the “changes would be voluntary, there would be no reduction in contractual hours and those who wish to continue a five-day working week pattern would be able to do so”.
He added: “We urge the RMT to call off this strike, meet with us and avoid any further disruption to Londoners. While we have been able to run more services than planned over the last 24 hours, we expect significant disruption to continue into Friday and the level of service we can provide will vary across lines, so customers should continue to check before they travel for the remainder of this week.”
The RMT is planning four more 24-hour strikes in May and June unless the dispute is resolved.

Services were reduced but not cancelled across most underground lines.

articles.title: What You Need To Know About Why London Tube Drivers Are On Strike
articles.author: HuffPost UK
articles.content:
So far in 2026, the transport trade union RMT has announced six strike dates for their members working on the London Underground (two each in April, May, and June).
This week (20-27 April), that’s meant commuters have had to deal with delays, cancellations, and reduced service on multiple Tube lines.
But why are the strikes happening in the first place?
Why are the 2026 Tube strikes happening?
They were announced after TfL offered some drivers four-day work weeks, which means that they can opt to work for longer hours over fewer days.
Currently, most drivers work a five-day work week. The four-day version compresses their hours across fewer days. It’s being tested on the Bakerloo line at the moment.
But the RMT says that the plan TfL has proposed might impact the safety of their drivers and passengers, and that it could mean drivers only get 24 hours’ notice before their shifts are announced. They also say TfL “U-turned” on negotiations.
In response, the TfL said the four-day is optional and that it’d improve the service’s reliability and flexibility.
Not all drivers are taking part in these strikes. Members of ASLEF, for instance, are not involved; over half of London Tube drivers are ASLEF members.
Here’s what the RMT, TfL, and ASLEF have have told HuffPost UK so far:
1) RMT
“Our objection to the imposed ‘fake four-day week’ is that it amounts to five days’ work compressed into four. This includes reduced flexibility over shift patterns, with the potential for only 24 hours’ notice of what shifts people will be doing, serious concerns from our members about shift length and resulting fatigue impacting safety in a safety-critical role like tube driving, and the fact that Transport for London has made no new offer despite months of negotiation,” a spokesperson told us.
“The strikes are going ahead because TfL said they would negotiate on all elements of the proposal and then U-turned, saying to us they would go ahead without any changes to their original proposals. That means RMT is in the position where we have nothing new to offer our members, leaving them no other choice than to take strike action.
2) TfL
Nick Dent, director of customer operations for London Underground, said: “We urge the RMT to call off this strike, meet with us and avoid any further disruption to Londoners. While we have been able to run more services than planned over the last 24 hours, we expect significant disruption to continue into Friday and the level of service we can provide will vary across lines, so customers should continue to check before they travel for the remainder of this week.
’We have set out proposals to the RMT for a four-day working week which are supported by the other Trade Union representing London Underground drivers. This allows us to offer train operators an additional day off, whilst at the same time bringing London Underground in line with the working patterns of other train operating companies, improving reliability and flexibility at no additional cost. The changes would be voluntary, there would be no reduction in contractual hours and those who wish to continue a five-day working week pattern would be able to do so.”
3) ASLEF
A spokesperson for ASLEF said: “We are surprised that the RMT has decided to take this action. The voluntary four-day week gives Tube train drivers an extra 35 days off every year, with rosters based on a 34-hour working week in return for some fairly minor changes to working conditions and moving to electronic, rather than paper-based, systems for booking on for duty. And, as it is voluntary, anyone who wants to keep working a five-day week will be able to do that.”

articles.title: The very miserable TfL rule that could cost us
articles.author: Yahoo News UK
articles.content:
It’s inadvisable to sing on London Underground services as you could land yourself with a fine. It’s courtesy of a Transport for London (TfL) byelaw “no person on the railway shall to the annoyance of any person shall sing” unless the transport body’s explicitly given you the green light to do so.
This covers everything from chanting to singing, and even performing on carriages and platforms. If you’re found to be doing any of these things, then you can be slapped with a fine and cautioned by a TfL member of staff.
But it doesn’t cover buskers as they’re safe under the London Underground Busking Scheme which caters to musicians to share their talents live in certain stations. These include Stratford, Piccadilly Circus, Marble Arch, and Victoria stations.
As a result the Tube has seen famous faces like Jessie J and Ed Sheeran belt bangers on the transport service. The killjoy rule serves to ensure that travellers are comfortable and ensure a calm and orderly travelling environment.
But it’s likely not to stop commuters from vocally enjoying themselves, especially after a few beverages. There are also other rules that are not well known to such as spitting on the railway and distributing anything promotional on the Tube.

articles.author: BBC
articles.content:
- Published
The second in a series of 24-hour strikes by London Underground drivers begins at midday on Thursday.
The strike by members of the Rail, Maritime and Transport union (RMT), which represents roughly half of drivers on the Tube network, is expected to cause travel disruption across the capital.
The union is in a dispute with Transport for London (TfL) over changes to the working week and said it was concerned about the safety impact of proposed shifts lengths. It said it had planned four more 24-hour strikes in May and June if the row was not resolved.
TfL said the industrial action was "completely unnecessary" and the proposed working week pattern was optional.
The industrial action will begin at 12:00 on Thursday and last for 24 hours
The Piccadilly and Circle lines will be closed entirely
The Metropolitan line will be closed between Baker Street and Aldgate
Central line services will not run between White City and Liverpool Street
Other lines that do run will be offering a significantly reduced service
Latest status updates here, external
Why are Tube drivers striking?
The RMT has rejected an offer for Tube drivers to voluntarily work a four-day week.
Under the proposals, most drivers would see their working week reduced from 36 hours to 35 hours, but their salary would remain the same.
The union said it was concerned about shift lengths, unacceptable working time arrangements and the possible impact of fatigue on safety.
The union it wanted a 32-hour week over four days, which would see drivers work three fewer hours each week for the same salary.
RMT official Jared Wood said: "TfL need to come forward with changes to their proposals for this dispute to be resolved."
Claire Mann, TfL's chief operating officer, said the four day week proposal "allows us to offer train operators an additional day off, whilst at the same time bringing London Underground in line with the working patterns of other train operating companies."
She added: "The changes would be voluntary, there would be no reduction in contractual hours and those who wish to continue a five-day working week pattern would be able to do so."

articles.title: United Kingdom to Brace Travel Sector as London Tube Strikes in 2026 Threaten Tourism, Economy and Visitor Experience - Travel And Tour World
articles.author: Travel And Tour World
articles.content:
London — one of the world’s most visited cities — is facing a significant travel disruption in 2026 as prolonged strikes by London Underground (Tube) workers continue to impact transportation across the capital. The strikes, led primarily by members of the Rail, Maritime and Transport Union (RMT) over a dispute with Transport for London (TfL), have not only frustrated daily commuters but now pose a substantial threat to tourism, travel plans and the broader UK economy. According to economic analysis, the cumulative effect of the strike action could see losses of up to £760 million by mid‑year if the walkouts persist into May and June.
For international travellers planning visits to London — whether for heritage explorations, cultural events, or business trips — the Tube strikes represent a real challenge that requires strategic planning. With central attractions like the British Museum, Tower of London, West End theatres and Buckingham Palace drawing millions of visitors annually, reliable transportation is critical. As the strikes ripple through the travel ecosystem, understanding their implications for tourism has become essential.
The current Tube strikes are rooted in a dispute between the RMT union and Transport for London over proposed changes to working arrangements — specifically a controversial plan to compress a traditional five‑day workweek into four longer days for some Tube workers. The RMT argues that this could increase fatigue and workplace risk, while TfL, under financial pressure, maintains that the change is voluntary and necessary for operational sustainability.
While other unions, including the Associated Society of Locomotive Engineers and Firemen (ASLEF), have supported the four‑day workweek concept, the RMT has pushed ahead with strike action. This has resulted in multiple 24‑hour walkouts affecting key lines such as the Piccadilly and Circle lines, with reduced services or suspensions even on lines that do remain operational.
Advertisement
The financial repercussions of the London Tube strikes extend far beyond a simple commuter inconvenience. According to estimates by the Centre for Economics and Business Research (Cebr), the combined cost of the Tube strikes — factoring in days lost by workers unable to reach their jobs, reduced output, and weakened consumer spending — could total between £390 million and £760 million by the end of the industrial action period.
This analysis considers only direct economic costs such as lost working days. Indirect impacts — such as decreased footfall in local businesses, increased road congestion, and reduced tourism bookings — could push those figures even higher. Retailers, hospitality operators and service industries that depend on commuter and tourist traffic are already feeling the strain; early evidence from industry groups suggests hospitality revenue in central London slumped by nearly 20 per cent during the most recent strikes.

For tourists, London’s Tube network is often the backbone of city travel. Millions rely on it to move between airports like Heathrow and Gatwick, major hotels, cultural venues, and iconic attractions. With services disrupted — and future strikes planned through May and June — visitors must reassess travel strategies.
Industry data indicates that hospitality bookings can plunge dramatically during strike periods, with some restaurants and pubs experiencing declines of up to 67 per cent in reservations. Tour operators warn that families and international tourists are cancelling or shortening stays due to fears of transport gridlock and unpredictable city mobility.

The strikes have also intensified debates on how London’s reputation as a tourist‑friendly destination could be affected. Tourism associations and business groups are calling for contingency plans, clearer travel guidance and expanded use of alternative transportation — from buses and coaches to river ferries and hired bicycles — to mitigate disruption for visitors.

With strikes coinciding with peak travel season, the impact on bookings and revenue could be substantial. Hospitality trade bodies have warned of “devastating” effects, with declines in footfall worsening existing financial pressures from broader economic conditions.

For travellers eager to explore London’s culinary scene, theatre districts, markets and historic neighbourhoods, this means planning ahead is critical. Many businesses have adjusted opening hours, provided online bookings and offered updates on access routes during strike days to support visitor planning.

Finally, travellers from outside the UK — particularly from Europe, India, the United States, and Australia — should monitor advisories from their home governments, as travel guidance can adjust based on evolving transport conditions. These advisories often provide practical tips on alternative routes and safety measures for navigating London during industrial action.
The ongoing Tube strikes underline broader issues around labour relations, infrastructure investment, and urban mobility in major global cities. London’s ability to host large events — from international conferences to sporting occasions — can be influenced by perceptions of transport reliability.
For the travel and tourism industry, a key priority lies in restoring confidence among future visitors. Should rail disputes continue without resolution, there is concern that London could see a decline in repeat tourism and longer stays — especially from visitors whose itineraries rely heavily on efficient public transit.
However, London’s enduring appeal — from the British Museum and Buckingham Palace to the vibrant multicultural food scene and parks — remains a powerful draw for travellers. With effective planning, communication from transport authorities and adaptive travel strategies, the city can continue to thrive as a leading global destination.

TfL chiefs 'baffled' by London Tube strikes as lines paralysed – see full list
Tube drivers have gone out on strike over plans to introduce a four-day working week, while Transport for London bosses say the industrial action is unnecessary
Commuters are facing severe disruption due two 24-hour Tube strikes this week over changes to drivers' working conditions - despite TfL claiming the changes are "voluntary" and "minimal".
Members of the Rail, Maritime and Transport union (RMT) walked out for 24 hours until midday on Wednesday and will strike again from the same time on Thursday, affecting services for the rest of the week.
Transport for London (TfL) urged passengers to check before they travel, as the industrial action led to widespread delays. Services on some Tube lines, including the Circle, Central and Piccadilly were suspended or part suspended, while there were severe delays on other parts of the network.

But TfL's Director of Customer Operations Nick Dent claims the planned changes for train drivers are "voluntary" as he says there was no need for the strike action, which is "frustrating" for travellers around London. He told LBC he was baffled by the walkout.
"We appreciate that it's frustrating. We have done everything possible to try and avoid the action,” he said. “What we've said to the RMT is rather than disrupt London with industrial action, work with us and the other trade unions involved to work through the details because we think the impact on train operators will be minimal.“

He said: “TfL need to come forward with changes to their proposals for this dispute to be resolved. There is absolute unanimity among our members that we have to fight these proposals.”
While RMT general secretary Eddie Dempsey also said ahead of the strike: “We have approached negotiations with TfL in good faith throughout this entire process, but despite our best efforts, TfL seem unwilling to make any concessions in a bid to avert strike action.
“This is extremely disappointing and has baffled our negotiators. The approach of TfL is not one which leads to industrial peace and will infuriate our members who want to see a negotiated settlement to this avoidable dispute.”

articles.title: Tube strikes were the least effective for years - here are five reasons why
articles.author: London Evening Standard
articles.content:
Sources within the transport authority said they could not remember any previous RMT strikes in which over half of the planned services continued to operate.
It was thought that the strike action could result in most trains being cancelled - but some of these busiest underground lines, such as the Bakerloo, Victoria and Northern lines, have managed to operate at around two-thirds of their normal service, resulting in only minor delays.
In comparison, every single line across the network was suspended during the strike between September 8 and 11, with only the Northern line able to open fully on September 9 and parts of four others running for brief periods.
As a result, Londoners were forced to either work from home or pack into Elizabeth line or London Overground trains, while Lime and Forest experienced a huge surge in people travelling on their rental e-bikes.
This walkout’s failure to bring the capital to a standstill suggests that the RMT union may be losing its power, with Thomas Turrell, the Conservatives’ City Hall transport spokesman, describing the data as a “bitter disappointment to the union barons who sought to paralyse London”.
Mr Turrell said: “The Conservatives created legislation to ensure this level of service as a legal minimum during strikes, which Labour promptly dropped - and as such, any strike which is more damaging to London than the one we have seen this week will be a blatant political choice by authorities.”
“Whilst it is a relief that the full damage of this strike did not come to pass, we must not ignore the fact that these strikes come only because the unions think that our weak Labour Mayor will capitulate to them.”
Read More
An RMT spokesman told The Standard: “Our strike is solid and reflects our growing presence in the driver grade in London Underground. TfL need to focus on revising the offer our members have overwhelmingly rejected to avert further disruption in the coming months.”
But why have the latest series of Tube strikes failed to make so much of an impact? Here are five reasons why.
RMT members are striking - but Aslef aren’t
Only around half of London’s 3,300 Tube drivers are members of the RMT.
Aslef has already agreed to a 35-hour week, which is being offered to all drivers on a voluntary basis, while the RMT wants drivers’ working hours cut to 32 per week with no reduction in pay.
Only train drivers have walked out
In September, all 10,000 of the RMT’s members walked out - but this week, it is only the drivers who aren’t working.
On that occasion, all staff were locked into a dispute over pay and working conditions. This included drivers, station staff and service controllers.
Service controllers play a similar role to that of an air traffic controller - regulating train movements, communicating with staff and customers during disruptions, as well as running signalling systems.
Their absence in September was the most important factor in determining whether lines could operate or not.
Shortly after those strikes, the pay dispute was resolved when the RMT accepted a 3.4% pay offer in November.
However, the specific issues surrounding Tube driver working hours and conditions were not addressed - hence the strikes this week.
Some lines unaffected
Only Tube lines have been affected by the action this week.
On this occasion, the Elizabeth line, the DLR, London Overground services and National Rail trains have all been operating a good service, providing a viable alternative for many passengers.
Around 33% more people than normal have used the Elizabeth Line this week, taking on many additional commuters as it passes through the middle of the capital - easing the issues caused by the part-suspension of the Central Line across its middle stretch between White City and Liverpool Street.
Overground use has also risen significantly, up 18%.
Flexible working
Throughout the strike action, Londoners have heeded TfL’s warnings about significant disruption. Across the whole week, TfL said that customer journeys were 12% down on normal across the whole network.
Officials confirmed a 13% drop in the number of contactless cards tapping in on Tuesday compared with the same day last year.
This equates to around half a million fewer travellers, a decrease from 3.9 million tap-ins last year to 3.4 million earlier this week.
The timing of the strikes has also helped - in the era of flexible working, people have been able to leave the office early to beat the worst of the rush or avoid the strikes altogether.
During the strike action in September, which ran all day as opposed to midday to midday, both the morning and evening rush hours were severely impacted, which has not been the case this time around.
Cycling and buses
TfL Director Nick Dent said that, despite the disruption, it is estimated that 88% of journeys in London still took place on Thursday compared to a normal day using all different modes of public transport.
Many commuters into London have switched to cycling, with TfL's bike hire scheme up 28%.
Operators like Lime, Forest and Voi have also seen a huge surge in riders, and helped by the beautiful weather, many with a shorter commute have been walking into the city.
There has also been a 6% increase in journeys taken by bus.
articles.summary: Sources within the transport authority said they could not remember any previous RMT strikes in which over half of the planned services continued to operate. It was thought that the strike action could result in most trains being cancelled - but some of these busiest underground lines, such as the Bakerloo, Victoria and Northern lines, have managed to operate at around two-thirds of their normal service, resulting in only minor delays.

articles.title: Tube strikes London April 2026 - Everything you need to know
articles.author: Daily Express
articles.content:
Tube strikes have caused chaos for London commuters this week, and a new 24-hour strike is set to wreak more havoc in the capital.
A second 24 hour strike began at midday on Thursday, April 23.
The RMT has rejected a proposal for Tube drivers to move to a voluntary four‑day week, although TfL says the strike is not necessary as the new working hours are voluntary.
As commuters grapple with severe delays and cancelled trains, the Express breaks down everything you need to know about strikes this week.
Read more: When do London Underground strikes end as capital faces more travel chaos
Read more: London commuters face more Tube strikes misery this week as 8pm warning issued
Are Tube strikes still on?
Yes, the tube strikes are still on.
RMT general secretary Eddie Dempsey said: "We have approached negotiations with TfL in good faith throughout this entire process, but despite our best efforts, TfL seem unwilling to make any concessions in a bid to avert strike action.
"This is extremely disappointing and has baffled our negotiators. The approach of TfL is not one which leads to industrial peace and will infuriate our members who want to see a negotiated settlement to this avoidable dispute."
Claire Mann, TfL's chief operating officer, said the four day week proposal "allows us to offer train operators an additional day off, whilst at the same time bringing London Underground in line with the working patterns of other train operating companies."
She added: "The changes would be voluntary, there would be no reduction in contractual hours and those who wish to continue a five-day working week pattern would be able to do so."
When are the next Tube strikes?
23–24 April (midday Thursday - midday Friday)
19–20 May (midday Tuesday - midday Wednesday)
21–22 May (midday Thursday - midday Friday)
16–17 June (midday Tuesday - midday Wednesday)
18–19 June (midday Thursday - midday Friday)
Full list of 11 lines closed on Thursday and Friday:
- Bakerloo
- Central
- Circle
- District
- Hammersmith & City
- Jubilee
- Metropolitan
- Northern
- Piccadilly
- Victoria
- Waterloo & City
When do Tube strikes end?
Tube strikes are often cancelled with very little notice — sometimes less than 18 hours before picket lines are due to form — because negotiations frequently continue until the last possible moment, meaning a strike can be called off while people are literally setting their alarms for the next day.
In January 2024, for instance, action was cancelled around 5pm on a Sunday, even though it was due to begin that evening and into Monday, yet disruption still followed because trains and drivers were not in the correct positions, and TfL cannot reset the network’s logistics overnight.
As of today, Thursday, April 23, the strikes remain scheduled, and reports indicate that no formal peace talks were planned between TfL and the RMT.
The current strikes will end on Friday, April 24, at midday.
Why are there Tube strikes?
The RMT has rejected a proposal for Tube drivers to move to a voluntary four‑day week, which would have reduced most drivers’ hours from 36 to 35 without affecting their pay.
The union argued that the plan raised concerns about longer shifts, unacceptable working‑time arrangements and the risk of fatigue compromising safety, and said it instead wants a 32‑hour, four‑day week that cuts three hours while keeping salaries unchanged.
RMT official Jared Wood urged TfL to revise its proposals to resolve the dispute, while TfL’s chief operating officer, Claire Mann, said the four‑day option would give drivers an extra day off and align London Underground with other train operators, stressing that the change would be voluntary and that those preferring a five‑day pattern could continue with it.
articles.summary: Tube strikes have caused chaos for London commuters this week, and a new 24-hour strike is set to wreak more havoc in the capital. A second 24 hour strike began at midday on Thursday, April 23. The RMT has rejected a proposal for Tube drivers to move to a voluntary four‑day week, although TfL says the strike is not necessary as the new working hours are voluntary.

articles.title: Transport for London joins drive to reduce staff sickness rates
articles.author: BBC
articles.content:
Transport for London (TfL) is stepping up efforts to cut employee absence as part of a government drive to keep people in work.
The transport authority has joined the Keep Britain Working Review - with mental health support being flagged as a key focus at TfL.
A report from 2025 found the transport body's overall sickness rate stood at 6.3%, accounting for almost 418,885 sick days. The figures also showed 6.6 million planned days off, which cover medical leave arranged in advance.
Dr Sam Phillips, TfL's head of health and wellbeing, said there was a "fine balance" between improving absence rates "but not at the cost of people feeling that they're coming to work when they shouldn't be".
Long‑term sickness made up the majority of days lost at TfL, with 286,673 days recorded. The average length of all sickness leave was 11.81 days.
The transport body says it is already taking action to support staff, including offering physiotherapy, addiction services and trauma‑focused counselling.
Phillips told the Local Democracy Reporting Service there was a balance to be struck.
"Sick days are costing the whole of the UK a lot of money, and that's one of the reasons we're involved in the prevention sprint, to look at ways to try and stop people from becoming ill in the first place.
"There is also another side to sickness absence, which is presenteeism.
"In organisations where you have very low sickness absence you may have high presenteeism where people are actually at work when they shouldn't be and they're unwell," she said.
Mental health was the leading cause of long‑term absence among TfL staff in 2025, accounting for 30% of cases.
Minister for Employment, Dame Diana Johnson, said: "I've been hearing about some of the programmes that TfL have around volunteer members of staff, helping other members of the staff who have perhaps experienced trauma in the workplace, providing support and help at the right level, and if people need something more professional they are referred on."
articles.summary: Transport for London (TfL) is stepping up efforts to cut employee absence as part of a government drive to keep people in work. The transport authority has joined the Keep Britain Working Review - with mental health support being flagged as a key focus at TfL. A report from 2025 found the transport body's overall sickness rate stood at 6.3%, accounting for almost 418,885 sick days. The figures also showed 6.6 million planned days off, which cover medical leave arranged in advance.

articles.title: UK’s Public Transport Chaos: London Tube Strikes Keep Commuters in Limbo as RMT Walkouts Spread – How Long Will This Disruption Last? - Travel And Tour World
articles.author: Travel And Tour World
articles.content:
Londoners are facing yet another wave of disruption on the London Underground as the RMT union’s ongoing strike action continues to wreak havoc on commuters. This 24-hour walkout, which began at midday on Tuesday, will last until midday Wednesday, causing widespread delays and cancellations across the capital’s Tube network. The impact of this strike is compounded by the fact that it will be followed by another 24-hour walkout starting at midday on Thursday. This means that disruptions will extend well into the upcoming days, further testing the patience of the city’s commuters and residents.
The strike, which has been organised by Tube drivers represented by the RMT union, stems from a dispute with Transport for London (TfL) regarding working hours and conditions. The immediate result of this industrial action has been the complete closure of the Circle Line, while several other lines have experienced partial suspensions. The strike has left many commuters in a difficult position, with some lines facing severe delays and others only minor disruptions.
Advertisement
Following the end of the walkout at midday Wednesday, minor delays are expected to persist throughout the afternoon, with full service not anticipated to return until the evening. This continued disruption is likely to affect daily travel, especially during peak hours when Tube services are most needed. As if the current strike was not enough, TfL has warned passengers to expect further complications with the additional 24-hour walkout planned for Thursday, which is expected to stretch into Friday evening.
As commuters already struggle to navigate the impact of this week’s strikes, TfL has issued advice urging passengers to check travel updates regularly to avoid unnecessary inconvenience. The strikes are not only affecting the Tube services but are also expected to have a ripple effect on other aspects of the city’s transport network, including buses and other services operated by Stagecoach. A separate 24-hour strike on Friday from 5am will add to the frustration for those who rely on public transport to get around London.
Advertisement
The situation looks set to worsen in the coming months as the RMT has announced additional strike dates in May and June. A total of four more 24-hour strikes are planned, further extending the disruption unless an agreement is reached between the union and TfL. These strikes will likely continue to affect commuters’ ability to rely on public transport for their daily travel needs.
The strike action is driven by a broader dispute between the RMT union and Transport for London over working hours and conditions. Although the primary issue in this dispute is related to the implementation of a four-day working week, other concerns have also emerged. According to union officials, the dispute is not just about reducing the working week; it also involves changes to annual leave and the length of shifts, which are seen as detrimental to workers’ conditions.
Advertisement
Advertisement
The RMT has stated that their members feel strongly about the proposals put forward by TfL, arguing that these changes are unsatisfactory and unfair. In particular, union leaders have emphasized that there is “absolute unanimity” among union members that the proposed changes need to be renegotiated in order to prevent further industrial action.
On the other side of the dispute, TfL has set out proposals aimed at resolving the issue. The plan includes offering Tube operators a voluntary four-day working week, which would provide an additional day off while maintaining the current contractual hours. TfL has emphasized that the changes would bring the London Underground in line with other train operating companies in terms of working patterns. The changes are designed to improve flexibility and reliability without incurring additional costs.
Despite the intentions behind these proposals, the RMT union has rejected them, and negotiations are still ongoing. TfL’s chief operating officer, Claire Mann, has said that the changes would have no impact on the contractual hours of workers and that anyone wishing to maintain a five-day work schedule would still have the option to do so.
The ongoing strikes are not only causing inconvenience to London commuters but are also affecting local businesses, especially in the hospitality sector. Pubs, restaurants, and shops in central London have expressed concern that the disruption to public transport will significantly impact their operations. With many workers and visitors unable to commute as usual, businesses that rely on foot traffic and local patrons are facing potential losses.
Emma McClarkin, the chief executive of the British Beer and Pub Association, highlighted the strain that the strikes would place on establishments already struggling with high operating costs. According to McClarkin, the disruption will be “acutely felt” by businesses that are already operating on thin margins.
As the ongoing disruption continues to affect London commuters and businesses, the outlook for the coming months remains uncertain. The union has announced that there will be four more planned strikes throughout May and June. These strikes are likely to prolong the already difficult situation for both passengers and local businesses, making it essential for all involved to find a resolution before further damage is done to London’s transport system and economy.
TfL has urged commuters to plan their journeys in advance and to check for updates regularly, particularly as the second round of strikes is set to take place from midday Thursday until Friday. With no resolution in sight, it is unclear when the dispute will end, and passengers will be able to enjoy reliable Tube services once again.

articles.title: Why are the Tube strikes happening and how much disruption will there be?
articles.author: London Evening Standard
articles.content:
They are the first walkouts in a series of six 24-hour strikes by drivers on the Tube.
But why are the drivers striking, when are they and how much disruption can passengers expect? Here is all you need to know.
What time are the Tube strikes?
As it stands, members of the RMT union are striking at the following times (all BST):
- 21–22 April (12pm Tuesday - 11:59am Wednesday)
- 23–24 April (12pm Thursday - 11:59am Friday)
- 19–20 May (12pm Tuesday - 11:59am Wednesday)
- 21–22 May (12pm Thursday - 11:59am Friday)
- 16–17 June (12pm Tuesday - 11:59am Wednesday)
- 18–19 June (12pm Thursday - 11:59am Friday)
Why is the strike taking place on the Tube?
Under the plans the majority of drivers would see their working week reduced from 36 hours to 35 hours – but they would work longer shifts on days they work.
The RMT argues the working day would be too long under the proposals, risking driver fatigue and potentially compromising safety.
The union instead wants to negotiate a 32-hour week over four days for drivers, meaning they would work three fewer hours each week for the same salary.
TfL is currently rejecting the RMT proposals, saying drivers do not need to take up the four day week offer and could remain on a five-day week if they want.
Members of the Aslef union have also already voted to accept TFL’s four-day week offer.
How much disruption is expected?
No service is expected at all on the Piccadilly and Circle lines during the strikes.
A reduced service will run across other lines but “significant disruption” is expected.
Any services that do run will be less frequent, very busy, and you may not be able to board the first train, TfL is warning.
Read More
No service is expected on the Metropolitan line between Baker Street and Aldgate.
No service is expected on the Central line between White City and Liverpool Street.
Outside of the specific strike times disruption is also expected.
While normal services will be expected until mid-morning on the Tuesday and Thursday, services will then begin to ramp-down before the 24-hour strikes.
Tube services that do run on Tuesday and Thursday will finish early. You should aim to have completed your journey by 8pm, TfL has said.
On the Wednesday and Friday, significant disruption will take place on all lines until midday.
Tube services that do run will start later than normal with no service expected before 7.30am on Wednesday and Friday.
In the afternoon on those days some disruption is expected until the evenings.

articles.author: The Mirror
articles.content:
London Underground tube strike update as Jubilee, Northern and Victoria lines hit by walkout
RMT union members are striking over TfL's proposed four-day working week, causing major disruption across the London Underground network this week, with parts of the Jubilee, Northern, Victoria, Bakerloo, Central, Piccadilly and Waterloo & City lines shut.
Multiple lines are experiencing disruption this week as Tube strikes affect London. The industrial action started on Tuesday at midday, as RMT train drivers accused Transport for London (TfL) of imposing a new, four-day working week.
The Rail, Maritime and Transport union (RMT) confirmed that its members will be on strike from 12pm for 24 hours on Tuesday and Thursday. RMT said TfL proposal would "compress" the working week and could also compromise safety. Today, passengers are being advised to anticipate disruption on all lines after midday.
No service is anticipated on the Piccadilly and Circle lines, the Metropolitan line between Baker Street and Aldgate, and the Central line between White City and Liverpool Street.
The Elizabeth line, DLR, London Overground, and tram services will be operating normally on strike days, TfL said. These services, however, are expected to be extremely busy.
TfL also provided the following information: "The vast majority of buses will be running normally throughout these strikes, but 7 bus routes operated by Stagecoach will be affected by separate strike action between 5am on Friday, April 24 and 5am on Saturday, April 25. Other buses will run as usual."
Here is a reminder of the Tube lines that will have no services during the strikes. Parts of the Bakerloo, Central, Jubilee, Northern, Piccadilly, Victoria, and Waterloo & City are shut. Strike actions are also planned for tomorrow.
Certain bus routes will also be disrupted by a separate strike. The overwhelming majority of buses will operate normally throughout these strikes. But, seven bus routes run by Stagecoach will be impacted by separate strike action between 5am on Friday, April 24 and 5am on Saturday, April 25. All other buses will run as normal.
The affected bus services are: 8, 25, 205, 425, N8, N25 and N205, reports the Express.
"We expect that the 25 and 425 will run a near normal service for most of the day throughout the strikes. The N8 will run a reduced route between Hainault and Liverpool Street at its usual frequency. The other affected routes are likely to be severely delayed and subject to cancellations," TfL said in an update on its website.
Commenting on the strikes scheduled for this month, union leaders stated that while the working week would technically be shorter in terms of days, the lengthier shifts could heighten driver fatigue.
They also expressed concern that the changes might enable management to extend maximum driving time, force drivers to start earlier or finish later, alter shifts with as little as one day's notice, and reduce flexibility for drivers wishing to transfer between depots. TfL branded the strikes as "completely unnecessary" and revealed it was presently testing a voluntary four-day week for drivers on the Bakerloo Line.
Claire Mann, TfL's chief operating officer, said: "We have set out proposals to the RMT for a four-day working week. This allows us to offer train operators an additional day off, whilst at the same time bringing London Underground in line with the working patterns of other train operating companies, improving reliability and flexibility at no additional cost. The changes would be voluntary, there would be no reduction in contractual hours and those who wish to continue a five-day working week pattern would be able to do so."

Multiple lines are experiencing disruption this week as Tube strikes affect London.

articles.title: Film London teams up with TfL and VCCP for "Act Like a Friend" | Film London
articles.author: Film London
articles.content:
News Story
It’s not every day our emerging filmmaker talent gets to work with leading advertising agencies and marketing budgets on campaigns that get seen by - and make a difference to - millions.
But that’s exactly what happened when Transport for London (TfL) teamed up with leading London agency VCCP, Film London alum. Producer Jamie Clarke of My Accomplice, up-and-coming Director Edem Kelman (also Film London alum.), and a whole host of crew drawn from Film London’s Equal Access Network, on TfL’s new "Act Like A Friend" video campaign.
The story is just such an inspiring journey of how London’s ecosystem came together to create this hard-hitting short film, that we felt we had to share it.
The story goes like this…
Launching during National Hate Crime Awareness Week (11-18 October), in response to the Mayor's commitment to improving safety and confidence for all passengers, TfL’s Marketing department commissioned VCCP to come up with a creative concept that highlighted the hate crimes being experienced by people across the transport network, and had real impact.
VCCP worked with My Accomplice, sharing a vision to bring fresh London voices and perspectives onto the campaign. The film, which is showing at cinemas across London and on ITVX, draws on three true stories of Londoners who’ve witnessed another passenger being targeted, and who have helped defuse the incident by engaging the targeted person in a conversation, as they would with a friend.
The film was directed by Edem Kelman, and produced by Producer, Film London Connect Mentor and Production Finance Market alumnus Jamie Clark from My Accomplice.
We spoke to VCCP's Simon Plant and Jamie about the genesis of the campaign and the short film, and how important it was to work with crew from Film London's network on the shoot.
How did you start working with TfL? And also with VCCP?
Jamie Clark: My Accomplice were approached as a producer due to us as a company working across feature film (scripted/unscripted) and commercial work. I was sent the initial script by Simon Plant at VCCP and loved the premise and the use of real peoples stories. It made the concept so powerful and a great jumping off point for finding a director. VCCP had a very bold vision for the work that we really connect with and naturally wanted to be a part of.
We thought of ways to amplify the campaign and one was to do a meaningful partnership with Film London. We have always as producers wanted to try and elevate new talent and this production provided a great opportunity. We worked with crew on the shoot and are taking part in the mentor scheme too.
Simon Plant: VCCP’s production arm Girl and Bear approached My Accomplice. Girl and Bear were very keen from the beginning to use this as an opportunity to bring new talent into the advertising space. They knew My Accomplice as a production company that understood commercials and could access talent that they would be unfamiliar with.
Talk about the film-making process – how did you find the Director?
Jamie Clark: VCCP’s brief was very inspiring and that was to send a short list of very interesting directors working in the short film to feature films space who could bring a unique take to this creatively and at the same time gain invaluable experience working in the short form/ advertising world with a brilliant agency like VCCP and a great client like TFL.
Edem Kelman was chosen and he co wrote the script with the agency and worked closely and brilliantly with the creative team at the agency throughout the production.
Simon Plant:We had already started working with a researcher to find real-life stories from Londoners across the Transport for London network. Girl & Bear briefed My Accomplice to find talent outside of the commercial world, and we focused our search on directors working in the short film or feature film space. We were also keen to speak with underrepresented talent.
We talked with three directors. The creatives and Transport for London felt that Edem Kelman’s skill in capturing humanity and a realistic vision of London life would suit the project, and Edem subsequently developed the script with the creatives
How about the crew?
Jamie Clark: We worked with some wonderful Film London crew on the shoot and it goes without saying that Film London crews will be the first people we contact on the next!
How long did it take to shoot and where did you do the post-production?
Jamie Clark: The shoot was two days across TfL network in London. We filmed on the overground at Crystal Palace, the tube at Charing Cross, and on a bus from Camberwell garage.
We worked with Lucy Berry at Final Cut on the edit and sound designer Michael Griggs on the sound design.
Were there any elements that surprised you or you found particularly noteworthy in the process?
Simon Plant: The enthusiasm for the project was immense. The collaboration and effort from everyone involved were extraordinary.
articles.summary: News Story It’s not every day our emerging filmmaker talent gets to work with leading advertising agencies and marketing budgets on campaigns that get seen by - and make a difference to - millions. But that’s exactly what happened when Transport for London (TfL) teamed up with leading London agency VCCP, Film London alum.

articles.title: Climate Crisis Advisory Group: Important signal from this new science panel, including CCAG emeritus member ...
articles.author: Climate Crisis Advisory Group
articles.content:
Important signal from this new science panel, including CCAG emeritus member Johan Rockström.

What stands out is the focus on credible, whole-of-government transition roadmaps to move beyond high-level commitments and tackle the structural barriers to phasing out fossil fuels. 

This is exactly where the conversation needs to go. We are no longer short of targets, we are short of delivery.

In an overshoot context, the challenge is not just decarbonisation in the abstract, but managing a rapid, orderly transition that aligns energy systems, finance, and political incentives with the realities of climate risk.

Science-led roadmaps, grounded in real economies and real politics, are essential if we are to turn ambition into implementation.
articles.summary: Important signal from this new science panel, including CCAG emeritus member Johan Rockström. What stands out is the focus on credible, whole-of-government transition roadmaps to move beyond high-level commitments and tackle the structural barriers to phasing out fossil fuels. This is exactly where the conversation needs to go. We are no longer short of targets, we are short of delivery.

articles.author: Prof. Mark Maslin
articles.content:
𝐍𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐡 𝐀𝐭𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐜 𝐜𝐢𝐫𝐜𝐮𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐬 𝐔𝐍𝐋𝐈𝐊𝐄𝐋𝐘 𝐭𝐨 𝐜𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐚𝐩𝐬𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐜𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐲 - 𝐝𝐞𝐬𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐞 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐦𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐚 𝐫𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐬.

The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a vast system of ocean currents that helps to distribute heat around the world. By transporting warm water from the tropics northwards and cold water back southwards, the AMOC keeps Europe warm and plays a role in controlling global rainfall.

IPCC has projected that the AMOC will decline over the course of the 21st century as the world warms.

IPCC says a “collapse” before 2100 is unlikely. 

However, some scientists have argued climate change could force the AMOC past a “point of no return” over the coming decades that could usher it towards a “shutdown” 𝒏𝒆𝒙𝒕 𝒄𝒆𝒏𝒕𝒖𝒓𝒚.  Note the words here - 𝒏𝒆𝒙𝒕 𝒄𝒆𝒏𝒕𝒖𝒓𝒚 - in more than 75 years time.

Carbon Brief interactive article sums up the science - and shows that the media and many climate activists are misrepresenting the science and creating hysteria - when we should be focusing on much more real and pressing issues caused by climate change - extreme weather events, food and water insecurity, sea level rise, and deteriation in human health.

Edward Hopkins, Climate Crisis Advisory Group, E3G, David Wilson, Stefan Rahmstorf, Fiona Harvey, Zack King, Andy Wilkins, Bill McGuire, Carina Fearnley, Geographical Association, Harriet Waters, Katharine Hayhoe, Corinne Le Quere, Roger Highfield, New Scientist, Penny Sarchet

articles.title: TfL signs £99.1M bridges and civil structures maintenance contract with M Group | New Civil Engineer
articles.author: New Civil Engineer
articles.content:
The award of the Bridges and Civil Structures Maintenance Contract was announced in February and followed a competitive flexible procurement process under the Procurement Act 2023.
The contract is structured as a five-year term, from 7 April 2026 to 6 April 2031, with an option to extend by a further three years, through to 6 April 2034.
It is valued at £99.1M, excluding VAT, and £119M including VAT.
The framework covers:
- The application of protective coatings to civils assets such as brick, masonry, concrete structures and steelwork
- Vegetation management (non -track side)
- Intervention activities to cable posts including replacement of defective cable posts
- Maintenance interventions to brick tunnel, covered way and girder maintenance
- Intervention activities to cable stiles
- Inspection planning and support services
- Cable draw pit maintenance
- Four-yearly interventions to assets
- Replacement of missing/damaged identification plates
- Fault response and reactive maintenance
“These services are critical in ensuring the safety of railway operations and the bridges and structures maintenance contract is pivotal in upholding safety standards and preventing accidents,” said the tender notice.

articles.title: London tube strikes: Full list of lines affected as second day of disruption begins
articles.author: The Independent
articles.content:
London tube strikes: Full list of lines affected as second day of disruption begins
- London Underground drivers, represented by the RMT union, are striking for 24 hours from midday on Tuesday 21 April and again on Thursday 23 April, with further action planned for May and June.
- The RMT union accuses Transport for London (TfL) of attempting to impose a new four-day working week, a claim TfL refutes, stating the changes are voluntary and aim to improve service reliability.
- On strike days (Tuesday and Thursday), services will wind down by mid-morning, with significant disruption from midday and lines finishing early; commuters are advised to complete journeys by 8pm.
- On the mornings following strike days (Wednesday and Friday), Tube services will begin later, with significant disruption expected until midday before normal service gradually resumes.
- Several lines, including parts of the Bakerloo, Central, Jubilee, Northern, Piccadilly, Victoria, and Waterloo & City lines, will have no service, though Elizabeth line, DLR, London Overground, and tram services will operate normally but are expected to be very busy.
